item.title: What to Know About the Case Behind Netflix's New True-Crime Docuseries The Trials of Karen Read
item.description: The controversial case took over social media from 2022 to 2024. Now, the two consecutive trials are at the center of a docuseries with the family of slain Boston police officer John O’Keefe at its center

media:content.media:description: John O'Keefe and Karen Read in The Trials of Karen Read

item.content:encoded:
On Jan. 29, 2022, Boston police officer John O’Keefe, 46, was found dead in the snow outside of his friend’s home in Canton, Mass. His girlfriend, Karen Read, was arrested and accused of second-degree murder and manslaughter, with authorities alleging that she ran over O’Keefe in her SUV while driving under the influence, then left him in the snow to die. Read pleaded not guilty, and her defense attorneys made the case that there was reasonable doubt as to whether O’Keefe might have been killed by a fellow police officer and not Read, seeding a widespread conspiracy involving Massachusetts public officials. 

The new Netflix docuseries The Trials of Karen Read, in which Read herself did not participate, features interviews with O’Keefe’s mother Peggy and brother Paul, plus key witnesses for the prosecution and jurors who served on the case. Michael Proctor, a former Massachusetts State Police trooper and the lead investigator on the case, narrates much of the documentary, which began filming during Read’s first trial and concludes with the final verdict and her acquittal. 

The docuseries has already proved divisive. Though O’Keefe’s family has said that they are “satisfied” with the result, Proctor’s involvement has generated criticism because he was fired in March 2025 from the Massachusetts state police after allegedly sending “crude and racially charged remarks” as well as “derogatory texts” about Read. Proctor later described the messages as “unprofessional and regrettable.” Here’s what to know about O’Keefe’s death, Read’s trial, and where the case stands today.

The night of O’Keefe’s death 

The party on the night of Jan. 28, 2022, was just like any other: Read, then 44, her boyfriend O'Keefe, and a group of their friends were drinking at the Waterfall Bar and Grill in Canton, Mass. Then they went to the home of O’Keefe’s fellow Boston police officer, Brian Albert. But no one ever saw O’Keefe and Read at Albert’s: “That night, there [was] a lot of people in my house,” says Albert, who would go on to testify against Read, in the documentary. “If John had come in either door, he would've been seen by everybody in the middle of the kitchen. John O'Keefe never came into my house.” It wasn’t until 4:23 a.m. on Jan. 29 that friends became concerned about O'Keefe's whereabouts. O'Keefe's niece called Albert's sister-in-law, Jennifer McCabe, to ask where he was. Read had asked the niece to check on him since O'Keefe had not come home that night and was not answering his cell phone. According to court documents, McCabe heard Read yelling, "John didn't come home. We had a fight." 

At 5:07 a.m., Read, McCabe, and another friend went out to search for O’Keefe. Read allegedly told her friends, "What if he's dead? What if a plow hit him? … I don't remember anything from last night, we drank so much I don't remember anything."

At approximately 6 a.m. Read saw O'Keefe dead in the snow outside Albert's house. An emergency responder who was on site after 9-1-1 was called testified that Read repeatedly said, "I hit him. I hit him." There was a crack in the tail light of Read’s car. The case against Read came together quickly: prosecutors claimed that Read must have struck him with her SUV while under the influence of alcohol, and then left him to die in the snow. But Read’s attorneys offered the possibility that she might have been framed, suggesting that O'Keefe might have been attacked inside Albert’s home. 

Police found a broken cocktail glass and pieces of a car tail light at the crime scene. After an autopsy was completed, the medical examiner ruled that the cause of death was blunt impact injuries to the head and hypothermia and that there were not "any obvious signs of an altercation or a fight." 

A strained relationship

In the time leading up to O’Keefe’s death, he and Read were reportedly experiencing difficulties in their relationship. The text messages between the two implied that they had had an argument on the night in question: at around 1 a.m. on Jan. 29, Read allegedly left O'Keefe a voicemail calling him a “f-cking loser" and saying, “John, I f-cking hate you." During this time, Read allegedly sent "flirty" text messages to Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives agent Brian Higgins. 

Read later admitted that things had not been perfect with O’Keefe, and even suggested that he was unfaithful to her during a trip to Aruba. "We argued," Read told Vanity Fair. "But was I abusive? Was I neglectful? Did I mistreat him emotionally or in any way? Or did we have ups and downs?" 

The first trial

Read was charged with second-degree murder, leaving the scene of a crime, and manslaughter in the death of O'Keefe. She pleaded not guilty to the charges of manslaughter, motor vehicle homicide, and leaving the scene of a motor vehicle collision causing death on Feb. 2, 2022. She was later arraigned on the new charges in O'Keefe's death and pleaded not guilty once again. Read was released on June 10, 2022 after her $100,000 bail was paid. 

During the May 2023 trial, Read’s defense attorneys, Alan Jackson and David Yannetti, alleged that O'Keefe was involved in a fight inside Albert's home, leaving O’Keefe beaten to death—citing wounds on his arms that allegedly resulted from being bitten by Albert's dog—with his corpse later being dumped outside. Read's attorneys added during a pretrial hearing that these actions could have been a cover-up by law enforcement to obscure any association with a murder. 

"Certainly the Massachusetts State Police is involved. There are people that were in that house that are involved," Jackson said via CBS News. "Brian Albert is involved. Jennifer McCabe is involved. The rest of the folks that were in that house, there's some level of involvement by every one of them. Every single one of them. We're not going to rest until we get to the bottom of exactly who's behind this cover-up." Albert has maintained that O’Keefe was never in his house, and he says in the docuseries that Jackson put a target on his back. 

Read said to reporters at the time, "We know who did it. We know. And we know who spearheaded this cover-up. You all know. I tried to save his life. I tried to save his life at six in the morning, I was covered in his blood. I was the only one trying to save his life."

The case goes viral

By August 2023, the case had attracted widespread attention online. Presiding judge Beverly Cannone had to address a requested gag order from the Norfolk District Attorney's office, which claimed that trial witnesses were being harassed. District Attorney Michael Morrissey released a video statement saying, "Conspiracy theories are not evidence. The idea that multiple police departments, EMTs, Fire personnel, the medical examiner, and the prosecuting agency are joined in, or taken in by, a vast conspiracy should be seen for what it is—completely contrary to the evidence and a desperate attempt to re-assign guilt."

The alleged witness harassment led to the arrest of blogger Aidan Kearney, who ran the website "Turtleboy News." Kearney was arrested on charges of witness intimidation related to the Read case, especially after he filmed himself confronting witnesses. One month before Read’s trial began, Kearney had recorded over 550 episodes of his Canton Cover-Up show, which led to an estimated income of $45,000 to $50,000 a month through his YouTube live shows during his coverage of the case. Kearney also had exchanged 189 phone calls with Read leading up to her trial, with Read reviewing and editing Kearney’s early reporting and supplying additional information about witnesses, per Boston Magazine. Messages also reportedly showed Read’s defense attorney David Yannetti encouraging Kearney’s livestreams.

In December 2023, Kearney was indicted on 16 criminal counts including witness intimidation, conspiracy to intimidate witnesses, and unlawful picketing intended to influence witnesses. Prosecutors alleged that people connected to the case were confronted at their homes, workplaces, and children’s sporting events. In May 2025, a judge dismissed six of the 16 counts. Kearney separately faced charges of domestic assault and battery, wiretapping, and witness intimidation connected to his former girlfriend, Lindsey Gaetani, but those charges were dropped in October 2025. 

Witnesses in the docuseries say the alleged intimidation has stuck with them. Colin Albert, Brian Albert’s nephew and a witness for the prosecution, says he still fears for his life. "I am scared every single day about somebody coming up to me, whether they try to attack me, whether they try to do something horrible,” he says. “I'm scared every day of my life for that."

Muddled evidence 

In March 2024, an FBI expert involved in a federal investigation into the case claimed that the prosecutor’s evidence of the broken tail light did not support the theory that O'Keefe died after being hit by an SUV. "The damage on the car was inconsistent with having made contact with John O'Keefe's body,” Read’s attorney Jackson said. “In other words, the car didn't hit him, and he wasn't hit by the car." 

The Massachusetts State Police also began an internal investigation into "a potential violation of department policy" by Trooper Michael Proctor, the lead investigator on the O’Keefe case. 

McCabe, who was with Read when she discovered O’Keefe’s corpse, testified on May 17, 2024 that Read asked her to Google how long it would take for somebody to die in the cold. Defense attorneys argued the Google search happened before O'Keefe's body was found; however, the conclusion after investigating the technology trails remained inconclusive, and if anything, pointed to the search being conducted after 6 a.m., when O’Keefe was discovered. 

The jury ended up without a verdict, leading to a hung jury and mistrial on July 1, 2024, after which Proctor was relieved of duty. 

Karen Read’s second trial

Read’s attorneys sought to dismiss two of the charges against her, with the legal team filing an appeal to the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court on Sept. 11, 2024.

O'Keefe's family provided a statement to WBZ-TV in January 2025 on the anniversary of his death, saying, "It has been 3 years since Johnny was senselessly taken from us. The void in our lives grows with each passing day, week, month and year. His absence is profound and we will continue to seek justice for him. He is always in our hearts."

Read’s next trial began in 2025, with deliberations starting on June 13, 2025. By June 18, 2025, the jurors had acquitted Read of second-degree murder, manslaughter while operating under the influence, and leaving the scene of an accident resulting in death. Read was convicted of driving under the influence of alcohol. Judge Cannone sentenced Read to one year of probation.

What’s next for Karen Read? 

Following the second trial, Read filed a lawsuit against Michael Proctor, Jen McCabe, Brian Higgins and other key witnesses, and later against the Massachusetts State Police and Canton Police. Four witnesses filed a defamation lawsuit against Read and Kearney. Many of these legal challenges remain open.

Read is set to launch a podcast in 2027 with her defense attorney Jackson. The duo are also reportedly working on a film script and a book together. Read maintains her innocence in the death of O’Keefe. 

"The O'Keefes never carried a pitchfork for me until I started getting support,” Read told Vanity Fair in October 2024. “You didn't speak to any media. Now you're giving interviews. You really just can't stand my rising from the ashes. The only thing that changed is I started to come from a position of power...I've reached the point that—John, if you can hear me—I've done everything I can. I don't think your family can be saved. They want to see me incarcerated for the rest of my life despite never seeing evidence while you were alive that I mistreated you. We were dating for two years, and I've since eclipsed those two years. I'm going on three, and I've got to save myself now."

The docuseries quickly skyrocketed to the top of the Netflix Top 10 and will surely revive interest in one of the biggest cases this decade to fascinate both the true-crime community and the general public.

item.title: Breaking Down the Ending of The Remarried Empress
item.description: How the K-drama builds to its fairy tale cliffhanger
item.content:encoded:
It’s hard to imagine The Remarried Empress appearing on a streamer other than Disney+. The K-drama plays out like a fairy tale. Adapted from a massively successful webcomic and webtoon of the same name, the series stars Hometown Cha Cha Cha’s Shin Min-a as the empress of a fictional Eastern Empire. As the poised, seemingly perfect Empress Navier, Shin wears over 70 princess-like costumes across the series’ 10 episodes. Her beau—Heinrey (Romance is a Bonus Book’s Lee Jong-suk), a playboy prince from the neighboring Western Kingdom—can turn into a bird. 

“People talk a lot about the music, the princes and princesses, the kings — that Disney feel,” says Mikyung (Michelle) Kwon, the CEO and President of Studio N, the Korean TV and film production arm of WEBTOON, and a producer on the series. “So I think we were fortunate that it all came together so well.” Studio N has worked with many global streamers, including Netflix (Sweet Home, Bloodhounds, Mercy For None), Disney+ (Vigilante), and Paramount+ (A Bloody Lucky Day), so The Remarried Empress’ partnership with Disney was not a given. 

“With this project, honestly—and I can say this—during development I wanted to go with whoever would give us the bigger budget,” says Kwon. “Because that really matters when you have to deliver this kind of output.”

The Remarried Empress’ source material

While many have characterized The Remarried Empress as a big risk for Studio N, and for the Korean TV industry more broadly, Kwon says she has never doubted the project, which started development in 2020. The story began as a popular 325- chapter web novel series, written by the Korean author Alphatart. In late 2019, a year after the web novel’s launch, a manhwa adaptation written by HereLee and illustrated by Sumpul started on WEBTOON. Before the launch of the TV series, the webtoon had around three billion cumulative views. According to WEBTOON, in the two weeks following the K-drama’s November 3rd premiere, global readership of the webcomic surged roughly 35 times what it was in the two weeks prior to the debut. 

Kwon may have had total confidence in a live-action Remarried Empress adaptation, but it was a hard sell to potential collaborators. “When I offered the role to one actor, I actually got the answer, ‘We’re all Korean, and it feels too awkward to call each other by Western names. I don’t think I can do it,’” she recalls, referring to the European-inspired setting of the story. Unlike Hollywood, which regularly adapts stories set in foreign countries and cultures, the Korean TV industry usually produces projects set within Korea or a Korean community. When K-dramas take viewers outside of Korea, they tend to do it from a Korean perspective.  

The Remarried Empress, filmed in the Czech Republic and Korea, and is the biggest budget ever for a Studio N series. “A lot of people around me said things like, ‘How on earth are you going to pull this off?’ or ‘Isn’t this a bit much? Isn’t this a gamble?’” says Kwon. “Even now, when you used the word ‘gamble’ today, I thought, ‘Right, I guess it was.’ But I don’t think I ever saw it that way.”

What is The Remarried Empress about?

The Remarried Empress has a slow start, but it picks up in the second half of its 10-episode run. When we first meet Navier, she is married to Emperor Sovieshu (Trauma Code’s Ju Ji-hoon). The two have been betrothed since childhood, and share a respectful, if not romantic, marriage. When Sovieshu rescues escaped slave Rashta (The Red Sleeve’s Lee Se-young) from brutal punishment or worse, he immediately falls for her damsel-in-distress charms. As the season progresses, and Rashta gets a taste for power, she works to drive Navier and Sovieshu apart.

The Remarried Empress was adapted into TV scripts by two writers: Yeo Ji-na and Hyeon Chung-yeol. Kwon had previously worked with them on Studio N’s 2023 action comedy film Brave Citizen, and thought it might be good to have both a male and female perspective in the scriptwriting process. “I believed the tension among the four leads was essential,” says Kwon. “I think of this story as a boxing ring — each of the four characters is one of the corner posts holding it up, and if even one post is weak, the whole thing collapses. With two male leads and two female leads, we really needed both of their perspectives.”

 

In her machinations, Rashta has the help of Albani (Lovely Runner’s Jung Young-joo), a conniving noblewoman whose family has fallen out of favor. Albani’s husband is in jail following an attempted coup, and she sees Rashta as an opportunity to finally get him released and restore power to their family.  

Navier, who prioritizes her duties as Empress above all else, tries to keep her marriage—and therefore the kingdom—from falling apart, but her efforts are in vain. When Rashta becomes pregnant with Sovieshu’s child, the Emperor decides to divorce Navier and marry Rashta so that their son will be a legitimate heir to the throne. His decision is informed by Albani’s revelation that Navier is infertile. 

We learn that when Navier and Sovieshu were children, Albani prepared cookies that induced infertility in those who consumed them per the request of the then-Empress. The cookies were prepared for a tea party to which all of the then-Emperor’s mistresses were invited, but a young Navier and Sovieshu stole a cookie each off of the table. While Rashta’s pregnancy proves that Sovieshu can still have children, Albani believes—or at least she tells Sovieshu—that Navier will never be able to have a royal heir. 

Navier and Heinrey fall in love

As Sovieshu continues to push Navier away, Heinrey draws her closer. The two began a penpal relationship at the beginning of the series. Heinrey sends notes to Navier in the talons of Queen the bird. Unbeknownst to Navier, Heinrey is the bird, as members of the royal family in the Western Kingdom have this secret, magical ability. First, Navier finds a safe confidante in Queen. Then, when Heinrey finally visits the Eastern Kingdom in human form, she starts to fall for Heinrey too. On his side, playboy Heinrey falls for Navier’s stoic grace immediately.

Heading into the adaptation, Kwon was most concerned about getting the bird right. “The first question every fan asks when they hear it’s being adapted is, ‘So what are you going to do about the bird? Is the bird going to be in it?’ We couldn’t separate the story from the bird, so we wrestled with that a lot,” she says. The Remarried Empress’ VFX team studied real-life birds, and incorporated both Lee Jong-suk’s mannerisms and Prince Heinrey’s costuming and coloring, to create the CGI character of Queen for Navier to interact with. 

Kwon says she told the CGI company responsible for creating Queen to pay special attention to the bird. “I told them,  ‘Our four actors are all brilliant, and every one of them will absolutely deliver. But our fifth actor is Queen, the bird. After all the hard work the four of them put in, Queen can’t look off. So please give Queen everything you’ve got.’ I called the head of the CGI company very, very often and kept pressing them: ‘This fifth actor cannot fall short.’ And I think that’s how we got the Queen you see today.”

Initially, Navier doesn’t allow herself the luxury of romantic feelings for Heinrey… until she overhears Sovieshu’s plan for divorce. When Heinrey’s older brother dies, Navier volunteers to travel to the Western Kingdom as an Eastern Kingdom delegate at Heinrey’s coronation. While there, she tells Heinrey of the divorce, and he asks Navier to marry him instead. She agrees, opening her heart to Heinrey.

A royal divorce and remarriage

Before Heinrey and Navier can marry, they must secure permission from the Eastern Kingdom’s courts. When Sovietshu petitions the courts to allow him to divorce Navier, he prepares a mountain of defamatory evidence to force her to go along with the divorce and demotion. However, to everyone 's surprise, Navier doesn’t dispute the divorce. Instead, she asks for permission to marry Prince Heinrey.

The court grants it, and Sovieshu flies into a fury. When a manipulative Rashta implies to Sovieshu that Heinrey and Navier have been carrying on a romantic relationship behind his backs for months, he throws Heinrey into the dungeons, and locks Navier in a palace room. 

Sovieshu begs Navier to take him back, telling her that he cannot rule the kingdom without her. Sovieshu tells Navier that he always planned to reinstate Navier as Empress following the birth of his child; a flashback of him telling Rashta the same thing confirms that this is true. However, it is too late for Navier, who has been disrespected for months. She tells Sovieshu it is over, and that she plans on rebuilding her life with Heinrey.

The Remarried Empress’ ending explained

Meanwhile, Lady Albani visits her husband in prison. He suggests they have Heinrey murdered, as his death would provoke war between the Eastern and Western Kingdoms. He predicts that the resulting bloodshed would drive the public away from Sovieshu and towards the Albani family’s leadership. 

But Lady Albani’s assassins are too late. Heinrey has escaped the dungeons in his bird form, having made a plan with Navier to meet on the night of the full moon. Navier uses a secret passageway in her palace to slip past Sovieshu’s guards. The lovers reunite, and manage to make it to safety in the Western Kingdom, with the help of Heinrey’s right-hand man McKenna (Agent Kim Reactivated’s Choi Dae Hoon), and Navier’s older brother, her ladies-in-waiting, and her bodyguard. 

The season ends with Heinrey and Navier happy together, with plans to be wed. But all is not well. Sovieshu is unstable, vowing to burn down everything Navier holds dear. Rashta, who is now Empress of the Eastern Kingdom, is giddy with her newfound power. She orders every last trace of Navier to be wiped from the palace. Lady Albani’s daughter worries that Rashta might soon abandon the Albani family, as they have outgrown her usefulness. 

Lady Albani’s insurance policy

Lady Albani reassures her daughter; she has collateral. When Rashta realized she would be Empress, she ordered the murder of her former slaver, Viscount Lotteshu (My Happy Ending’s Park Ho-san), as well as the murders of Lotteshu’s son and his baby grandson, aka Rashta’s own child. 

Before coming to the palace, Rashta had a baby with Lotteshu’s son. Lotteshu uses the existence of the baby to blackmail Rashta for months. Now that she is pregnant with Sovieshu’s child and has a chance to be Empress, she vows to destroy anything that could endanger her position. Albani had Lotteshu’s son killed, but she spared the child. She knows that, if Rashta tries to disown the Albani family, the baby can be used to force her hand. If The Remarried Empress gets a second season, Lady Albani will continue to play a major role in palace politics.

The Remarried Empress Season 2

While there has yet to be official word on a second season of The Remarried Empress, a continuation of the story seems likely. There is still much of the source material’s story left to adapt—Navier doesn’t even know that Heinrey is a bird yet—and the series has done very well on Disney+. According to the streamer, The Remarried Empress became the most viewed local original premiere of all time on Disney+ globally, just three days after its launch. Meanwhile, an upcoming anime adaptation, slated to launch in 2027, could drive more interest towards other versions of the story. 

Kwon did not confirm a second or third season continuation of the story, but she did speak about the thought process behind the first season’s pacing. “If this does well, the story could continue into Seasons 2 and 3. So we agreed to cover as much as we could in the most entertaining way within about 10 episodes,” she says.

Looking back on the release of The Remarried Empress Season 1, Kwon hopes remembers the Korean public’s pre-premiere concern that global audiences would respond to a Western-inspired Korean fantasy series. “There were a lot of worries that it would feel to them the way it would feel to us if Western actors put on a Korean gat and hanbok and acted in a Korean palace setting,” she says. “When two cultures merge like that, there’s an unfamiliarity, a sense of dissonance. We thought Asian actors in a Western look might come across as awkward. But what I found from the reviews is that people don’t feel that at all. Nobody’s reviews are about Asian ethnicity or being Korean—they’re just about the story.”

item.title: El Niño Is Strengthening. Here’s Where Its Effects Are Already Showing Up
item.description: Warming in the Pacific is easing weather risks in some places but making them worse in others. Here’s what to look for now and in the weeks ahead.

media:content.media:description: A man paddles over a flooded road during a king tide in Mill Valley, California, on Nov. 24, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
The National Weather Service’s Climate Prediction Center sent out an advisory Monday that El Niño continues to strengthen as forecasters record ocean warming and atmospheric disruptions globally. 

“Chances for a historic event exceeding previous El Niños dating back to 1950 … are now ~60%,” it said.

Read more: What An Early Polar Vortex Combined With El Niño Means For Winter Weather

In an update on a weekly report from Nov. 12, the advisory showed more than a 79% chance of remaining strong to very strong through January–March 2027. The impacts of the event, however, are already present across the globe with above average temperatures and atmospheric anomalies over parts of the eastern Pacific Ocean.

The advisory comes as Thanksgiving week brings heavy rain, coastal flooding, and mountain snow to both coasts, elevating flood risks in California and Florida.

What is El Niño and how is it affecting the U.S.?

El Niño refers to the warm phase of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) cycle, and it occurs every two to seven years when surface waters in the eastern and central tropical Pacific become unusually warm, reaching at least 0.5 degrees Celsius above average. 

This ocean heat is released eventually into the atmosphere, and influences atmospheric circulation, temperatures, precipitation and other weather events around the globe.

Though the phenomenon is relatively common, this year’s El Niño has earned headlines for being among the strongest of its kind on record, partially because it's arriving on top of an ocean that is already warmer than it used to be.

Andrew Kruczkiewicz, senior researcher at the International Research Institute for Climate and Society at Columbia University, tells TIME that the effects of El Niño are region-dependent—which is why it is both associated with warmer, drier winters in the North, and wetter winters in the South, ice storms across the southern Plains.

“The impacts from El Nino across the U.S. are not uniform—El Nino does not lead to everyone seeing above average temperatures for winter or everybody seeing above average rainfall or everybody seeing below average rainfall,” he says.

 Risper Nyairo, assistant professor of environmental studies at Davidson College, calls it a “seesaw system” that depends on the pressure systems in each region.

“The whole idea behind this is really the pressure—pressure changes with the temperatures of our waters,” she says. “So if you are in a low-pressure zone, those tend to be warmer areas, which encourage air to rise and condense and form clouds and precipitation. If you are on the opposite side of it, which is a high-pressure zone, then your winds are sort of sinking, which means precipitation is not forming, and you get a drought.”

But some of these impacts are already rearing their heads, showing how the systems are strengthening and could ripple across the world.

Near Ecuador’s Galápagos Islands, off the coast of Peru, sea surface temperatures show an anomaly of +10 degrees Celsius, according to meteorologist Ryan Maue, meaning the ocean surface at that specific location and time of year is 10 degrees warmer than the long-term historical average.

“This is now a Mega El Niño,” Maue said of his findings on X.

High tides in California and Florida

The effects of El Niño are being seen in California, where a mixture of seasonal “king tides” combined with an unusually strong El Niño and large Pacific swells are driving near-record to record coastal water levels and flooding across California this week.

King tides are unusually high tides caused by the alignment and positions of the moon and sun. El Niño has raised coastal water levels, increasing the risk of flooding when those tides arrive.

San Francisco set a November tide record Tuesday, and the National Weather Service (NWS) on Wednesday warned of 20- to 25-foot waves in northern California that could potentially break onto highways. 

It also predicted “numerous road closures” in San Francisco on Wednesday, claiming there could be up to 2.7 feet of flooding above ground level in coastal regions.

In Central California, Santa Cruz temporarily closed its beaches and wharf, and local officials issued evacuation warnings covering roughly 200 coastal homes.

NOAA’s Los Angeles tide gauge recorded more high-tide flooding days than in any previous year in its record.

Potential drought relief in the South

El Niño's strengthening, according to NOAA, is likely to bring a wetter-than-average winter to parts of the southern United States, particularly the Southeast, which has been plagued by drought throughout 2026. 

Roughly two-thirds of the region was abnormally dry or in drought as of the U.S. Drought Monitor’s briefing Nov. 17.

NOAA said in mid-November that much of the Southeast has a 50% chance or greater for above-normal precipitation during winter—a probability that could increase with a strengthening El Niño. This relief is already beginning, with coastal storms developing off the coast of Florida, Georgia, and South Carolina this week.

“We are expected to have more precipitation, and we are seeing some of that in Florida, where some locations have reported receiving precipitation that is greater than a year's worth of rain within a day or two,” Nyairo says. She says that this drought relief in some regions is a rare “positive” to El Niño this year.

But with drought relief comes elevated risk of flooding over the winter—one people in low-lying regions should take seriously.

“I would say you know if you've seen the map and you are in a location where you think there might be above-average precipitation, you should be taking the warning seriously, especially with flooding,” she adds.

item.title: The Push to Free a Princeton Scientist From ICE Detention Is Growing
item.description: ICE detained Eva Yi Xie on her way home from a neuroscience conference. Her lawyers are challenging her detention in federal court.

media:content.media:credit: Hannah Beier—The Washington Post via Getty Images
media:content.media:description: Nassau Hall on Princeton University's campus is pictured in Princeton, New Jersey, on March 9, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detained a Princeton University doctoral candidate on Nov. 19 at an airport in Arlington, Virginia. Her colleagues, classmates, and lawmakers are calling for her immediate release ahead of Thanksgiving Weekend.

Eva Yi Xie, a Chinese national, was detained at the Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport as she departed from an annual conference of the Society for Neuroscience. Xie’s lawyers say that she was not presented with a warrant.

She was later taken to the Caroline Detention Center in Virginia, a court filing says. U.S. District Judge Anthony Trenga ordered the federal government to respond to a petition challenging Xie’s detention by 5 p.m. E.T. on Wednesday. In the meantime, he ordered ICE not to transfer or remove Xie from the Eastern District of Virginia.

Read more: Trump Opens Door to Immigration Deal. Democrats Want Proof He's Serious

According to court documents, Xie, 24, came to New York on a travel visa with her family in March 2016. Four months later, Xie’s mother applied for asylum. The family’s case is still pending, with a hearing scheduled for January 2028. Xie was granted work authorization and does not have any criminal history. 

Kerry Doyle, a lawyer who represents Xie, tells TIME that Xie has received “unprecedented” support from Princeton, as well as the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where Xie earned her undergraduate degree in 2024. She says that there is an effort to collect letters of support in order to facilitate her release.

“We have this incredibly talented student—and by all accounts, an incredible person—who studies neuroscience. She has a very great future, and we're arresting her at the airport for no reason,” Doyle says.

In a statement shared with TIME, an ICE spokesperson says that a pending asylum application does not confer legal status and that Xie never held “valid authorization to study in the United States.”

“Xie was admitted to the United States on a temporary basis on March 16, 2016, but chose to violate our nation’s laws by refusing to depart by the required date of September 15, 2016,” the spokesperson says. 

Democratic Senator Andy Kim of New Jersey, where Princeton is located, wrote on X on Monday that his office has been in touch with the school, Xie, and DHS in an effort to get more information and get her home.

“It's heartbreaking to see her detained and turned into another example of this administration's cruel immigration policies,” he said. 

Representative Bonnie Watson Coleman, a Democrat who represents Princeton University’s congressional district, said her office is closely following this case.

TIME has reached out to both offices for additional comment.

About 250 people showed up to a “Free Eva” rally at Princeton University on Monday in support of Xie. The organizers put together a phone bank to urge supporters to contact their federal representatives on Xie’s behalf.

Brody Lab, a neuroscience research group at Princeton, announced Xie’s arrest in a social media post last week and has since urged followers to contact congressional lawmakers to advocate for her prompt release. It says that Xie messaged the lab’s Slack channel for help when she got detained.

Rodney Priestley, the dean of the Graduate School at Princeton University, said last Friday that Xie’s detention was “distressing.” The university has provided legal counsel to Xie and remains in contact with Xie’s family.

Xie’s PhD adviser Carlos Brody told the Associated Press in an interview on Tuesday that Xie called into a weekly lab meeting to thank her coworkers for their support and is in “remarkable spirits.” 

Adrian Bondy, a research scholar in the lab, told AP that even in detention, Xie “wants the science to continue and is thinking about scientific ideas.”

Xie is not the first researcher arrested by ICE. Science reported that Di Liu, a chemistry assistant professor at Arizona State University with a valid work visa, was detained by ICE in July at an airport on his way to a scientific conference in Nashville, Tennessee. A few days later, he was released without explanation. Last year, Tufts researcher Rumeysa Ozturk was detained by ICE in Cambridge, Massachusetts. She decided in April 2026 to voluntarily leave the U.S. 

ICE arrests at U.S. airports

Two days after Xie’s arrest, ICE officers detained a father and daughter at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as passengers boarded an Alaska Airlines flight to Los Angeles. A viral video captured the moment when Mexican immigrant Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza and his daughter, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, were arrested. It showed Hernandez Mejia pleading for help before being dragged out of the jet bridge. 

The recent arrests continue a trend seen throughout the Trump Administration’s second term. Stateline reported that there was a nationwide goal of 2,000 ICE arrests a day; a senior Department of Homeland Security (DHS) official told NBC News that officers were averaging 20 to 40 arrests a day at U.S. airports as of August.

Since May 2025, ICE has been obtaining traveler information through the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) through a previously undisclosed data-sharing program, according to records obtained by the watchdog group American Oversight. The New York Times reported that the program gives ICE access to the names and birth dates of passengers whom the TSA believes may be subject to arrest.

On July 21, two plainclothes ICE agents arrested Chantal Morales Rojas, a 27-year-old from Ecuador, at the jet bridge at Denver International Airport. The next day, ICE arrested Ethiopian Berhanu Kibret, a University of Maryland School of Pharmacy instructor returning from a conference where he received a teaching award, at the University of Maryland at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport.

“It's a desperate attempt to hit numbers for the sake of numbers,” Nayna Gupta, the policy director at the American Immigration Council, tells TIME. 

The Trump Administration has also broadened its use of administrative warrants. Previous Administrations used such warrants to arrest people who were already in deportation proceedings. More recently, they have also been used in cases involving immigrants who are actively applying to renew their immigration status.

“In the past, people like that have never been prioritized for deportation if they pose no other public safety threat, given that they're taking steps to get into compliance with the law,” Gupta says.

“Our policy right now is to go after the worst of the worst,” DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said during a congressional hearing last week. “When we encounter someone here illegally, I am required to find out who they are.”

Backlogs and processing delays in the immigration system can put immigrants at risk of losing legal protections while their applications are pending, Gupta adds.

ICE agents have also been granted the authority to make arrests without a warrant in certain circumstances. For example, if they have probable cause to believe someone is in the country without legal status and is likely to escape if not immediately arrested. Gupta says that authority has been abused in previous immigration operations.

President Donald Trump has recently acknowledged that some immigration enforcement policies might be “too tough.” At the same time, he promoted Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration crackdown, to White House Chief of Staff. 

Less than a week after Democrats won a majority in the House and Senate during the 2026 Midterm Election, Mullin told reporters that Trump had encouraged him to work on immigration reform with the incoming Congress.

item.title: Trump Administration Unveils New Tariffs for China, the European Union, and More
item.description: The Trump Administration proposed sweeping new tariffs on 14 major trading partners, threatening to reignite global tensions.

media:content.media:description: President Donald Trump holds up a chart while speaking during a “Make America Wealthy Again” trade announcement event in the Rose Garden at the White House on April 2, 2025.

item.content:encoded:
The Trump Administration on Wednesday proposed sweeping new tariffs on 14 major trading partners, including China and the European Union, threatening to reignite global trade tensions.

China is set to be hit with the highest rate, facing tariffs of up to 20% on most covered goods. The rate could potentially rise to 40% if Beijing fails to honor the trade truce agreed upon between Beijing and Washington last year.

The European Union also faces a proposed tariff rate of 15%, accounting for certain existing duties, which could rise to 20% if existing trade agreements are not honored.

The proposed tariffs follow an investigation led by U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer’s office into what it described as unfair trade practices and excess manufacturing capacity that have placed American manufacturers at a disadvantage. The levies are meant to discourage excess capacity and production in sectors that “are unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce.”

A spokesperson for the European Commission told TIME it will “study the findings” of the report shared by the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR), but pushed back against any suggestion of Europe’s contribution to excess manufacturing. 

“We strongly reject the premise that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity. To the contrary, Europe is among those most exposed to overcapacity,” the spokesperson said. “The E.U. and the U.S. share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action.”

The European Commission will continue engaging with the U.S. Administration on the implementation of the joint trade agreement signed August 2025, the spokesperson said. “Under the Joint Statement, the 15% all-inclusive ceiling applies to E.U. goods. We expect any measure from this investigation to respect it in full, including when combined with existing duties,” they added.

The U.S. tariffs also target other major economies, including key allies Japan and South Korea, which face rates of up to 15%. India, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Vietnam, Taiwan, and Bangladesh are also included in the sweeping tariffs unveiled on Thanksgiving eve. The levies for these countries remain between 15% to upwards of 25%, with the notable exception of Vietnam, which may face tariffs of up to 35%. Further determinations concerning Mexico and Norway are still being considered.

The Trump Administration also announced a separate proposal seeking to increase tariffs on Brazil, targeting the country's sugar and aircraft exports.

Read More: Why the Trump Administration Is Being Accused of Interfering in Brazil's Election

The Trump Administration said it would impose the tariffs under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which permits the government to investigate unfair trade practices abroad and impose tariffs via the executive branch through its findings. The Administration previously announced two investigations in March as it sought ways to revive the tariffs struck down by the Supreme Court in February. 

“The 301 is a very powerful tool, empowering the executive branch to act against other countries when they find something that can arguably be described as an unreasonable discriminatory burden and restrict U.S. commerce,” Kathleen Clausen, a professor at Georgetown Law, tells TIME. She points to the fact that there have already been seven investigations by the USTR under the second Trump Administration, while there were only three during former President Joe Biden’s term.

Despite the sweeping proposals, Greer played down concerns that the new tariffs could disrupt the global economy.

“We’ve talked to our trading partners about this—they know what we’re proposing,” Greer told CNBC. “I think a lot of this is baked in, and I don’t think any of these would actually take effect earlier than a couple months from now.”

The earliest the Administration expects the tariffs to take effect is January 2027, with the proposals first subject to a public comment process and hearings. Any “interested persons” have until Jan. 5, 2027, to submit written comments or requests to appear at the hearings, alongside a summary of their proposed testimony.

Anyone can theoretically submit a request for a hearing or a written comment, says Clausen. “Businesses and related workers' groups that are principally affected by these actions are the type of expertise and constituency that would typically be invited to provide oral testimony at the hearing.” In those instances, “by law, the USTR must respond to the comment, not individually, but en masse, where they must address those comments in their determination.”

However, she notes that even if there is strong opposition amongst these consultations that may not deter the office of the USTR to go ahead with the implementation of these tariffs.

Beijing, ahead of the announcement, reiterated its opposition to "trade wars" and dismissed allegations that it was contributing to global manufacturing overcapacity.

"The so-called 'overcapacity' is ​a ⁠false issue, and China opposes using it as an excuse for political manipulation," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said, urging the world's two largest economies to maintain stable relations.

“A way of seeing what happened today is that this is a way to put pressure on our trading partners to be tougher on China,” argues Clausen.

“The USTR's feeling is that trading partners have not come to the table prepared to take enough action to combat these problems, either their own or directly with China over the years, and so stronger action was needed to be taken,” she says.

The latest tariff proposals, with their heightened focus on China, come just days after Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping struck a friendly tone during the President's visit to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. The two leaders joined Russian President Vladimir Putin for a historic trilateral sit-down. Trump and Xi are expected to meet again in December, when Trump hosts world leaders in Miami for the G20 summit.  

Clausen points out that under Section 301, the U.S. government must request a consultation with other foreign governments where these tariffs could be used as a bargaining chip in future trade negotiations.

“This is an effective time for the Administration if it wants to try and get a deal with these partners in an upcoming meeting when they're together,” she says. “We're in this period of feedback on whether these rates are the right rates for these particular countries, but whether these tariffs materialize, and what kind of exceptions will be built in, remains to be seen.”

Trump reignites global tensions with renewed tariffs push

Upon returning to the White House, Trump used tariffs as a hallmark of his protectionist agenda with the announcement of “Liberation Day” in April 2025 which saw a wide-range of sweeping tariffs on major global economies.

Although in February the Supreme Court struck down these tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, or IEEPA, it set the tone for the types of economic policy the second Trump Administration sought to pursue. 

Trump has also sought to use tariffs as a tool of economic pressure during trade negotiations. He notably threatened Europe with levies of 50% in May 2025, before reaching a joint agreement the following month that concluded with a 15% tariff ceiling for most E.U. exports.

Most recently, following a breakdown in negotiations with Canada, the U.S. introduced 50% tariffs on approximately $20 billion worth of Canadian goods, which Canada then reciprocated. The countries remain engaged in a contentious trade war with no clear path to a deal.

The President has also taken to utilizing tariffs to pursue other policy objectives. In January, he threatened to tariff U.S. allies if they didn’t support his push to annex the semi-autonomous Danish territory of Greenland. The annexation row was settled in September when Denmark, the U.S., and Greenland signed a security deal, expanding U.S. military access to the semi-autonomous territory, without compromising its sovereignty. 

While the Trump Administration favors tariffs, the practice remains deeply unpopular with Americans. An NBC News exit poll following the Republicans’ major losses in the midterm elections found that 66% of voters believed Trump’s tariff policies had hurt the national economy.

item.title: Breaking Down the Ending of Love in Disguise
item.description: The romantic comedy K-drama follows a female detective who goes undercover as a male secretary to investigate a murder
item.content:encoded:
In an era that’s seen the K-drama industry shift focus toward more stories of suspense, thriller, and crime, the romantic comedy Love in Disguise marks a return to a familiar K-drama trope.

The series, streaming on Prime Video stars Squid Game’s Yim Si-wan as Yoon Yi-joon, the heir apparent to the powerful Taekang Group. When Yi-joon’s secretary, Han Eun-yeong (Perfect Marriage Revenge’s Jung Yoo-min) ends up dead in Yi-joon’s office, the chaebol son becomes a prime suspect in her murder. 

To investigate, the police decide to send an undercover officer into Taekang Group and Yi-joon’s inner circle. However, the easiest in—installing someone as Yi-joon’s new secretary and bodyguard——doesn’t quite fit the candidate the police have in mind. Kang Jae-hee (Business Proposal’s Seol In-ah), a former special forces officer turned cop, is a woman, and Yi-joon is looking for a male personal secretary. That being said, with her short haircut, masculine dress, and husky voice, Jae-hee is often mistaken for a man. Jae-hee’s team decides to go for it.

At first, the notoriously untrusting Yi-joon keeps Jae-hee at an emotional distance. However, as Jae-hee proves that she will risk her life to protect her charge, Yi-joon's walls begin to crumble. He starts to develop feelings for Jae-hee, under the assumption that she is a man. As they spend more time together, and Jae-hee realizes that Yi-joon was not responsible for Eun-yeong’s death, Jae-hee begins to fall for Yi-joon too. But can their relationship survive the secrets she’s hiding?

Who killed secretary Han Eun-yeong?

Heading into the season finale of Love in Disguise, the villain has become clear. Yoon Mi-jin (Hong Eun-hee), Yi-joon’s eldest sister, has been funnelling billions of won from Taekang Group into a slush fund for years. While Yi-joon was not sure who was behind the slush fund, he knew it existed. When he asked Eun-yeong to help him investigate who was taking the money, the secretary got caught in the crosshairs. When she discovered that Mi-jin and Na Man-seok (Jo Seung-yoon), Yi-joon’s uncle, were working together to pull money into the slush fund, they had her killed.

But Eun-yeong’s brutal death just makes Yi-joon more desperate to find out who is behind the plot. With the help of Jae-hee, his best friend and lawyer Kim Si-hyeon (Crash Landing on You’s Kim Jung-hyun), Taekang Group secretary Lee Hye-jeong (Yeon Woo), and Jae-hee’s police colleagues, Yi-joon discovers Mi-jin’s guilt. Before she is caught, Mi-jin has her uncle killed, and also tries to take out Yi-joon, in an attempt to stay undetected. Jae-hee and Yi-joon are both shot trying to protect the other, but survive. At a Taekang Group board of directors’ meeting, an injured Yi-joon presents the evidence against his sister. She is arrested, and taken away.

How Love in Disguise fits into the tradition of gender-bending K-dramas

Love in Disguise is adapted from a web novel called Why You Don't Know It's a Girl?, written by Lee Ah-yeon and Ryu Do-ha, but the premise taps into a rich history of gender-bending storytelling within K-drama and elsewhere. Shakespeare popularized gender-bending romance in an English theater tradition that we still see on the stage today, but contemporary, on-screen examples of gender-bending romance tend to show up most frequently in East Asian drama. 

The 2007 series Coffee Prince, one of the first Korean dramas to draw in a global audience, stars Gong Yoo as food empire mogul Choi Han-gyeol, who falls for Koh Eun-chan (Yoon Eun-hye), a “tomboyish” woman pretending to be a man in order to get a job at Han-gyeol’s café. Other examples include You’re Beautiful (2009), Sungkyunkwan Scandal (2010), Empress Ki (2014), Love in the Moonlight (2016), and The King’s Affection (2021). The trope almost always features a woman pretending to be a man, though 2019’s The Tale of Nokdu sees its male protagonist pretending to be a woman. 

In Love in Disguise, Yi-joon’s discovery that Jae-hee has been lying about her gender comes in Episode 8. Jae-hee is stabbed while protecting Yi-joon, and she is rushed to the hospital. When a doctor refers to an unconscious Jae-hee as a woman, Yi-joon is shocked. He stays by Jae-hee’s side until she wakes up, and confronts her about the lie. The reveal causes a hiccup in their relationship, as Yi-joon views Jae-hee’s deception as confirmation that his feelings are unrequited. Meanwhile, Jae-hee is torn between confessing her feelings to Yi-joon and maintaining an emotional distance as an undercover police officer.

By series’ end, Yi-joon and Jae-hee have confessed their feelings to one another. The major obstacles in their relationship have more to do with Jae-hee’s position and Yi-joon’s fear that Jae-hee will be injured or worse while trying to protect him rather than either character’s gender identity.

Is Love in Disguise a queer romance?

While the Korean TV industry has produced some dramas centering explicitly queer characters (e.g. Love in the Big City), and some BL dramas (e.g. To My Star, Semantic Error), the industry has yet to produce a mainstream drama that centers a romantic relationship between two people of the same gender. For a global audience that has access to queer romance like Skam, Bad Buddy, Heartstoppers, and Heated Rivalry, it can feel like the K-drama industry—a global leader in romance TV—is falling behind in this kind of romance storytelling. And, in a country where 56% of residents view homosexuality as "morally unacceptable," according to a 2025 Pew Research Center survey, there is still a long way to go when it comes to LGBTQ+ rights, as well as on-screen depiction of queer characters and relationships.

Love in Disguise could be read as heteronormative; the apparent queerness of Yi-joon and Jae-hee’s love erased by the knowledge and eventual reveal that Jae-hee is a woman. But for viewers looking for a queer romance, Love in Disguise can easily be read as such. Personally, I don’t think the queerness in Love in Disguise can be completely waved away. In the show, when a photo of Yi-joon and Jae-hee kissing hits the presses, and a journalist asks Yi-joon if he is gay, he answers that his sexual identity depends on the preferred gender of his lover. He is attracted to Jae-hee, whatever her gender may be. The queer identity inherent in Yi-joon’s confession arguably makes Love in Disguise queer love story. 

Love in Disguise is also notable for the ways in which both of its leads subvert gender norms, and are supported in those subversions in the world of the show. Jae-hee doesn’t change her gender performance to go undercover as a man; her gender performance already skews traditionally masculine. Jae-hee’s way of dressing, styling, and expressing herself is accepted by the loved ones in her life, including her parents and her male co-workers. They do not try to change Jae-hee into a more feminine version of herself. Meanwhile, Yi-joon does not mind playing the role of the protected rather than the protector. Though he does act as a protector to Jae-hee in some moments of mortal peril, it is not because of a sense of masculine pride but rather because he cannot stand to lose the person he loves. 

Does Love in Disguise have a happy ending?

When it comes to the Taekang Group plot, there is much that is sad about the ending. Yi-joon is appointed the new CEO of the company by his emotionally withholding father, Yoon Tae-sik (Choi Jin-ho). But the betrayal by his sister, who was like a mother to Yi-joon following the death by suicide of their own mother, looms large. When Yi-joon visits Mi-jin in jail, she has no remorse for the people she has killed, or for trying to kill her own brother; she claims everything she did was for the Taekang Group. Likewise, their father takes no accountability for the cutthroat competition he encouraged in his children that helped create the circumstances for Mi-jin’s plot.

However, for the first time in a long time, Yi-joon is not alone. He has Jae-hee by his side, and she vows never to leave it. They gift one another couple rings, and are ultimately approved of by Jae-hee’s loving parents. Meanwhile, Jae-hee and her colleagues, who were in danger of being fired from the police force for their secret investigation, are publicly recognized. The corrupt police captain who helped cover for Mi-jin’s machinations, and was ready to let Jae-hee’s boss take the fall for it all, is fired. Jae-hee’s boss is promoted, and Jae-hee’s department is stronger than ever. Si-hyeon, who is kept busy driving Yi-joon to pick up Jae-hee from work, is also given a promotion. He also finally convinces Hye-jeong to give a romantic relationship a chance.

The show ends with Yi-joon and Jae-hee on a date inspired by a “heart-fluttering” dream Yi-joon had when he was in a coma. They frolic in a field, happy and together.

item.title: The ‘Red Flags’ Behind Nvidia Customer Megaspeed
item.description: Corporate records reveal a complex web of companies connecting a major Nvidia customer to historical Chinese state investment.

media:content.media:description: Megaspeed International's office in Singapore on Nov. 10, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company that became one of NVIDIA’s largest clients in Southeast Asia, grew out of a corporate network with links to Chinese state entities that should have raised “red flags” for NVIDIA and its partners, according to experts in international finance and Chinese corporate governance. 

Corporate records and open-source data obtained by TIME reveal that Megaspeed had a complex financial and corporate structure that obscured ties between three separate Chinese state entities and Megaspeed’s former parent company, 7Road Holdings Ltd. While the total investment from Chinese state entities amounted to a small minority stake, it was enough to qualify 7Road as a “state-invested enterprise” under Chinese law. 

A review of the convoluted maze of holdings shows that the affiliated companies share directors, registered addresses, and common naming conventions—patterns that experts say should have been noted by the U.S. Commerce Department, NVIDIA, and banks doing due diligence on the U.S. chipmaker’s sales to Megaspeed. 

“Nvidia should know who it's doing business with because of the reasons for sanctions,” says Jason Sharman, a professor of international relations at Cambridge University and an expert in China and offshore finance. “If that involves looking all the way through to the end of the chain, that's something they should do, and at least that's something they're legally required to do.”

Megaspeed, a computing company registered in Singapore with operations in Malaysia, was rebranded in 2023, shortly before it emerged as a key NVIDIA partner, and before Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive, began her affair with NVIDIA chief Jensen Huang. The data obtained by TIME on its corporate structure was initially collated by Quantifind, an AI-powered risk intelligence company. 

“Megaspeed’s historical ownership connections to Chinese entities, the involvement of offshore holding companies, and the subsequent changes in its corporate structure raise legitimate questions about the extent of its independence,” says Graham Bailey, who spent over a decade in financial crimes analytics and compliance at Wells Fargo, and is chief operating officer at Quantifind. “These connections do not, by themselves, establish wrongdoing or continued control. But they underscore why examining ownership records alone is insufficient.” 

NVIDIA, 7Road, and Megaspeed did not respond to a list of questions requesting comment. 

Megaspeed’s ownership history

Prior to Megaspeed’s 2023 rebrand, its parent company, 7Road Holdings Ltd., received indirect minority investment from three Chinese state entities: The State Council (China’s central government cabinet), the Wuhan State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission (an agency of local government), and the Hubei Provincial People's Government, according to corporate records TIME reviewed. 

In total, these Chinese entities held an indirect 1.9% stake in 7Road Holdings Ltd., Megaspeed’s former parent company. It is unclear if the remaining 98% hold any further Chinese state investment. The minority investment arrived via an offshore entity registered in the British Virgin Islands, which was owned by a Chinese state-linked fund called Shanghai Baohu Investment Management Center. 

The links were buried in a complex matrix of corporate entities and name changes. Megaspeed was separated from 7Road Holdings Ltd via a series of corporate handovers. In March 2023, its Hong Kong arm, 7Road International HK Ltd, transferred away the Singapore company 7Road International Pte Ltd to an offshore entity in the British Virgin Islands called Huang Le Ltd, named after Alice Huang. The original Singapore company was renamed Megaspeed.

“The ownership appears complicated by design, not accident,” said Justyna Gudzowska, a former U.S. Treasury sanctions official, and executive director of the anti-corruption organisation The Sentry. “The multiple layers of companies; successive ownership changes; indirect, historical connection to a minority Chinese state invested entity; and overlapping directorships and office addresses are red flags that would have warranted enhanced due diligence on the part of any U.S. company doing business with Megaspeed.”

An expert in international finance who formerly worked for a large American financial institution told TIME that if the Chinese connection were known, it would have made Megaspeed a “risky client” and led to a risk intelligence report being commissioned by any US bank doing business with it to uncover such red flags.  

The red flags

Five different entities across this matrix of companies share a naming convention: their monikers begin with trees or plants (Maple, Poplar, Hawthorn, Malus, Osmanthus), and end with “Vale.” The network’s footprint stretches from southeast Asia—spanning Singapore, Hong Kong, China, and Malaysia—to the Caribbean, with entities incorporated in the mostly opaque jurisdictions of the British Virgin Islands and the Caymans.

In two cases, these companies share addresses. In the first, businessman Kang Wei (Alice Huang’s associate, and the builder of a billion-dollar AI data-center network in China) was linked to one “Vale” company which shared the same Hong Kong address with 7Road's international HK.

In the second, Megaspeed’s Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix, allegedly conducted business with Apex Enterprise Solutions, a company that reportedly functioned as an Alibaba procurement unit—and also shared the same address as Alibaba’s local offices. Alibaba was added to the Pentagon blacklist in June this year, restricting the military and defense contractors from doing business with it, due to its alleged links to the Chinese military.

A complicated corporate structure 

One of the figures that emerges from this complicated web of holdings is a little known Singaporean businessman named Tan Yong Pong, who goes by James. He is the current director of Megaspeed, and also reportedly a director of Speedmatrix, which is linked to Alibaba. 

In November 2023, after a corporate reshuffle, Huang Le Ltd sold its stake in Megaspeed to Swiftdata, which remains its owner today. Tan is linked to both Megaspeed and Swiftdata. 

This complex structure is common for Chinese companies. It's at least as much for escaping Chinese regulations as for “hoodwinking the outside world,” opines Sharman. “But of course it does have the added benefit that it can make it difficult for foreigners to work out who actually owns this thing.”

China is now one of the largest users of offshore vehicles, according to two experts. “Offshore holding companies are often used to obfuscate the true ‘beneficial owners,’" John Cassara, who spent six years with the U.S. Treasury Department’s  Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), wrote in an email. “That is the intent. They want to make it as difficult as possible for investigators (and perhaps journalists) to follow the money trail.”

NVIDIA’s due diligence

Nvidia’s compliance team told the New York Times last year it had looked into Megaspeed and determined it was “wholly owned and operated by a company based and headquartered outside China, with no China shareholders”.

Jodi Vittori, a Georgetown University professor specializing in corruption, illicit finance, and U.S. national security, said NVIDIA’s ties to Megaspeed were troubling. “The lack of even basic due diligence on the firm Megaspeed and its associated firms is deeply alarming,” Vittori says. “That a company with so many red flags was nonetheless permitted to acquire such important chips could have significant national security ramifications for years or even decades to come.” 

A statement from the U.S. Department of Commerce to TIME said: "Commerce is enforcing export controls more strongly than ever before and has concluded some of the largest cases in history against export control violators. This is in stark contrast to the previous administration which approved several thousand licenses to entity listed parties and allowed the H20 to be exported to China without any restrictions.” 

The department did not respond to specific questions about Megaspeed. It pointed to six enforcement cases since August 2025—involving charges or arrests of 16 individuals accused of illegal chip smuggling to China—saying they “collectively cover billions of dollars in smuggled semiconductors.” 

“In all these cases, DOJ and Commerce have worked together to stop the illegal activity and bring the perpetrators to justice,” the statement added.

However, new congressional disclosures of BIS (Bureau of Industry and Security) license requests between December 2025 and April 2026 show NVIDIA sought approval to export hundreds of thousands of advanced chips to China, which included “requests for the export, re-export, or transfer (in-country)... to multiple companies identified as Chinese Military Companies” by the Department of Defense’s blacklist in June. The NVIDIA requests precede the addition of some of the companies to this blacklist. 

NVIDIA self-certified every transfer request as having a “low risk of diversion.” These requests were approved, not shipped. The disclosures raised questions from Democrats and Republicans about BIS and NVIDIA’s due diligence and risk assessment. A spokesperson for NVIDIA told the New York Times that NVIDIA’s shipments, while authorized by the U.S. government and legal, were halted from shipping to China, and that Nvidia “did not and will not” ship an H200 (advanced chip) to the company linked to Megaspeed, or any other company.

Following the release, BIS added Megaspeed, Swiftdata, Speedmatrix and Apex Enterprise Solutions to its Entity list, restricting exports to them without federal permission. The Entity List flags companies that “have been involved, are involved, or pose a significant risk of being or becoming involved in activities contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States.” Prior to this update, BIS had not added any new entities to this list in a year. 

Since the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as chief executive on Nov. 23, NVIDIA added in its statement that its Board has formed a “National Security and Export Control Committee comprised solely of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks,” and “commencing a search to fill a new position, Chief Compliance Officer”. 

In a previous statement, Megaspeed told TIME it “conducts legitimate and lawful business” and that the company had retained external legal counsel to conduct an internal investigation. 

“Megaspeed designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate,” the statement added.

item.title: What Time Should You Eat Thanksgiving Dinner? Here’s What Etiquette Experts Say
item.description: Serving times are a hotly-debated topic as we approach Thanksgiving Day. TIME spoke to etiquette experts for guidance on how the celebrations should unfold.

media:content.media:description: People share food at the dinner table during Thanksgiving.

item.content:encoded:
As households across America prepare to gather for their Thanksgiving celebrations, there’s one question at the forefront of hosts’ minds: what time should dinner be served?

A quick glance on social media will tell you that it’s a hotly-debated topic, and one that people have firm opinions on.

Lifestyle expert Martha Stewart’s online publication conducted a poll in 2024, asking readers what time Thanksgiving dinner should start. More than 34,000 people joined the conversation, with the majority of respondents (13,586) saying the meal should begin between 2 to 3 p.m., local time. Stewart is also a proponent of these timings, telling the Today show last year that she believes dinner should be served at 2 p.m., as “people are hungry” and are likely already starting to “circle the kitchen.”

But preferences can vary by household. In a Pew Research Center survey carried out in 2024, 38% of respondents selected between 3-6 p.m. as their preferred time to have Thanksgiving dinner, with 36% of respondents choosing the 12-3 p.m. slot. Only 11% said they would choose to have their dinner served after 6 p.m. A YouGov survey conducted in 2013 also found the majority of respondents said they start eating dinner between 3 p.m. and 6 p.m.

So, what is the best time to sit down and start the Thanksgiving meal? In search of an answer, TIME spoke to etiquette experts for guidance on how the celebrations should unfold.

Etiquette experts on what time Thanksgiving dinner should be served

Diane Gottsman, an international etiquette expert and founder of the Protocol School of Texas, says that in order to best accommodate most guests and have a productive flow to the day, “generally around 2 o'clock is a good time.”

An early mid-afternoon meal such as this can suit a variety of guest’s needs, she adds. If they’re traveling, it leaves ample time to arrive and enough time toward the close of the day to head home at a reasonable hour. For children, she says, that time can be factored into napping schedules and it may also suit people with shift work.

For households hosting elderly family members and friends, it’s better to avoid a later dinner time, so that people do not have to travel home after dark, Gottsman says.

However, not even etiquette experts are in complete agreement on timings, as every household is run differently.

For Lisa Lyons, a wedding planner and certified etiquette adviser, a later dinnertime is preferred.

“As someone who hosts Thanksgiving every single year, and given my professional background, I'd say the sweet spot is between 4-5pm,” she says.

This schedule enables the host to invite guests over at staggered times throughout the early afternoon, before the main event, she says. “I'll tell my guests an arrival time within 10 or 15 minutes of each other. This way, it allows me to properly offer them a glass of wine or something to drink and have some one-on-one time to speak with them,” she adds.

A later serving time can also alleviate some of the stresses facing the Thanksgiving host, Lyons argues.

“All of the preparation and cooking takes time, and so [a 4-5 p.m. start] prevents them from having to wake up at the crack of dawn to start their preparation,” she says, insisting that a late afternoon start time still allows plenty of space to avoid guests heading home too late into the night.

“Any later would cut a little too close to bedtime for some guests, especially if they have to traverse back to their home or hotel,” she says, emphasizing that she wouldn’t suggest serving dinner after 5 p.m. for this reason.

How to navigate Thanksgiving activities and sporting events

For some households, a lot of the Thanksgiving Day schedule will revolve around sitting down to watch parades taking place in cities across the country. “Our family likes to watch the [Macy's] Thanksgiving Day Parade, and then we love to watch the Westminster Dog Show after that,” says Lyons. “My children will want to help or contribute, so we'll take turns in the kitchen.”

This year, however, the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed to Saturday, due to concerns over expected bad weather.

Another staple in some American households is football. With three NFL games scheduled to take place this Thanksgiving from the early afternoon into the night, it could be that some guests will want to stay close to a screen at certain times.

However, etiquette experts are adamant that this shouldn’t impact what time dinner is served.

“I don't care if you're a diehard fan, you can take a few minutes to come sit at the table. Your host prepared a nice meal,” says Gottsman.

Childhood traditions can shape how different households manage Thanksgiving

A lot of adults may well base their dinner schedule on what they witnessed and experienced in their own households growing up.

Lyons acknowledges that her preference for a late-afternoon serving time likely stems from the fact that is what she experienced as a child. “I think probably you inherit your own family traditions, and that's certainly what I've done in my case” she says, joking that her eldest daughter “could not even fathom” eating earlier in the day the way her friends at college do.

By contrast, August Abbott, an etiquette expert at JustAnswer, says that she ate dinner at midday sharp growing up, but has since switched to a later time to better suit her household’s schedule. However, she notes there is a welcomed nostalgia in continuing traditions when you can.

"You get to relive memories you had of every Thanksgiving when you're sitting down and doing something that was done when you were six years old, so it kind of enhances the day,” she says.
