item.title: People Are Getting Worse at Handling Uncertainty
item.description: Having an "intolerance of uncertainty" is linked to developing anxiety, depression, and other conditions.

media:content.media:credit: Photo-Ilustration by Chloe Dowling for TIME (Source Image: mariannehope/Getty Images)

item.content:encoded:
Living with the unknown isn’t always easy. Not knowing if layoffs are headed your way or whether you’ll be able to afford rent would be difficult for anyone. But when the pressure of the unknown becomes so intense it interferes with daily life, this “intolerance of uncertainty,” as psychologists call it, becomes a risk factor for mental-health disorders, primarily anxiety and depression. 

Now, in a paper in JAMA Psychiatry, psychologists find that this trait rose in North America from 1992 to 2023. Using data on college students in about 140 studies, the researchers found a gradual rise at first, then a steeper one starting around 2012. The results mirror increasing trends of symptoms of anxiety and depression among young people, suggesting that they are linked not just to rising awareness of mental illness but also to a change in our underlying ability to handle uncertainty about the future.

How young people’s mental health has changed

Rates of anxiety and depression in young people in the U.S. and the U.K. have been rising for some time, studies have found. Some researchers have suggested that increased awareness of mental-health disorders has contributed to increased diagnoses. Others have speculated that economic hardship or social media have played a role. 

“Some authors have argued that 2012 was an inflection point, in part because mobile phone technology became so widespread among young people in the early 2010s,” says Jeroen van Baar, an epidemiology researcher at Boston University School of Public Health and an author of the new paper. One idea is that smartphones insulate us from uncertainty, to some extent, by providing information on demand. Spending time on a smartphone can also be a coping strategy to deal with the discomfort of uncertainty, but might be only of limited reassurance in reality. 

While the hypothesis that phones are involved needs more investigation before it’s clear whether it explains the trend, he says, “what our paper adds to this discussion is that it's not just the anxious or depressive symptoms that change around that time. It's also this underlying process of intolerance of uncertainty.”

A less-explored risk factor for anxiety

Intolerance of uncertainty is assessed using questionnaires asking people to rate how much they relate to statements like “I can’t stand being taken by surprise” or “I always want to know what the future has in store for me.” Psychologist Mark Freeston of Newcastle University in the U.K., who was part of the group behind the first questionnaires, still remembers the conversation more than 30 years ago in Montreal when he and his colleagues discussed the idea that intolerance of uncertainty could be a vulnerability factor of its own. 

They were wondering about the cognitive underpinnings of generalized anxiety disorder. “Current wisdom at the time was that worry was problem solving gone wrong,” he says, “and we'd come to the conclusion that people with generalized anxiety disorder, dominated obviously by worry, knew how to solve problems.” They didn’t reach the point of acting on that knowledge, however, because they were overwhelmed by trying to cover every possible outcome, for instance. 

The concept went on to be used in a stream of studies over the next few decades. Psychologists and other researchers found that intolerance of uncertainty reflected an important aspect of mental health that transcends individual diagnoses. “Then the pandemic came along,” says Freeston, “and suddenly the rest of the world discovered that the world is not certain. As if it ever had been—but everyone was under the belief, particularly in first-world countries, at least, that people had control over their lives.” A new wave of research assessed how intolerance of uncertainty affected people’s health during a highly uncertain time. 

The new study does not cover the effects of the pandemic in detail, says van Baar. “We only have one, two, maybe three years of potential COVID effect in the data.” But work from other groups suggests that this period had a substantial impact on the mental health of young people in particular.

Freeston, who was not involved in the new study, speculates that the rise it documents has to do with a different kind of change, one that started much earlier. “I don't actually believe that the world got objectively worse in a North American context at the time when you start seeing those increases,” he says. “I'm not convinced that the world certainly became more dangerous or more threatening. I think people had access to more information, and they relied less on their own [experience].” 

For his part, in future work, van Baar hopes to continue exploring how a natural human behavior—trying to predict what happens next, and suffering when accurate predictions are difficult—interacts with the features of the world we live in. “I think there are signs from macroeconomics, from geopolitics, and from other domains like the job market under AI and so on, that suggest that the world that young people grow up in today is quite uncertain, potentially more uncertain than it was, say, in the '90s. This is a contentious claim, but I think there's some evidence pointing toward that,” he says.

How to live alongside uncertainty

“One of the things that we learned during the pandemic is that you cannot ‘information’ your way out of uncertainty,” says Freeston. “As soon as you have more information, you haven't eliminated uncertainty. You've just moved what you're uncertain about.” That means more information can lead to a great sense of anxiety: Reassurance seems forever out of reach.

He divides information into four categories, with the first being things you actually need to know today, like whether the grocery store is open and whether your flight is canceled. The second is information about the bigger picture behind current events, which you can get from journalists and experts but which will also bring some additional uncertainty to the table. “You may feel more informed, but you're less certain. It comes at a cost,” he says.

 

“The third category of information is essentially probably the great majority of the digital world, and this is clickbait, it's hooks. This is people ostensibly providing information, but it's for their benefit. So it's not about you; it's about them…that is a category you really don't need,” he says. 

The fourth category is what he calls “rebalancing information”: the kind that’s closer to home or involves causes you’re close to. During the pandemic, he explored regional newspapers and found something interesting. “What you found if you looked at those news sources, even in the worst part of the pandemic, was the local petty criminals were still being petty criminals, and animals were still being rescued. Children were winning prizes. Charities were doing amazing things.” 

Consuming more information from this category—and less from people you don't know or trust online—may be one way to ground yourself in an unpredictable world. “I think one of the ways that we can dial down the impact of uncertainty is people becoming more selective in their use” of information, Freeston says.

item.title: The Holiday Tradition of Pretending Our Families Get Along Perfectly
item.description: "Maintaining an illusion of perfect family harmony can come at a considerable emotional cost," writes Jillian Sanders.
item.content:encoded:
Imagine ending a romantic relationship after years of unresolved conflict. The arguments have become familiar, the resentments have accumulated, and conversations that once offered the possibility of understanding now go nowhere. Eventually, you accept that the relationship isn't working and decide to go your separate ways.

Now imagine being told that you're still expected to spend the holidays together every year: to arrive with a gift, exchange pleasantries over dinner, smile together for photographs, and ask about each other's lives as though the years of conflict between you never existed.

We would find this arrangement peculiar, unhealthy, even cruel, if it involved a former romantic partner. Yet when the person sitting across the table is a relative, we consider it perfectly normal.

Hollywood has long reinforced this expectation through countless holiday movies in which dysfunctional families gather, dredge up old grievances, and somehow reconcile before the credits roll. From The Family Stone and Home for the Holidays to Four Christmases and This Christmas, these movies offer what real life so often doesn't: the promise that even the deepest family divisions can be healed.

In reality, many families gather year after year without ever confronting the issues that divide them. They uphold traditions, exchange expressions of love, and maintain the appearance of togetherness, only to return to their strained relationships once the wreaths have come off the doors and the Christmas trees have been carried to the curb.

But maintaining that illusion of perfect family harmony can come at a considerable emotional cost. 

According to a 2023 American Psychological Association survey, 43% of American adults said holiday stress interfered with their ability to enjoy the season. We often attribute that stress to money, travel, and competing obligations. But what about the pressure to pretend our family relationships are healthier than they actually are?

A friend of mine, now in her late forties, has a complicated relationship with her older sister, in part because they experienced two entirely different childhoods. When their parents divorced, her sister was 17 and preparing to leave for college. My friend was just nine, left to navigate two households, custody arrangements, and the emotional aftermath of her parents' separation.

While her older sister remembers a relatively stable upbringing, my friend recalls years of uncertainty and upheaval. As adults, their memories of family life are so different that conversations about their childhood often escalate into heated phone calls, followed by months of silence.

For my friend, the most painful part is not that she and her sister remember their childhood differently, but that her sister, who was largely spared the upheaval of their parents’ divorce, has never fully acknowledged what her younger sibling endured. Because her sister never experienced the same instability, she seems unable to appreciate how profoundly those years shaped my friend’s life. The divide between them isn't simply a matter of conflicting memories. It's the frustration of having one's experiences dismissed by someone who wasn’t there to witness them.

Perhaps it's not surprising, then, that a YouGov survey found that 24% of American adults are estranged from a sibling, with 18% of those saying they had simply grown apart. After all, growing up together doesn't guarantee that siblings will remain close, or that the bond they shared in childhood will endure into adulthood.

Parents, meanwhile, are often caught in the middle. As they grow older, many grow weary of the disagreements between their adult children. Understandably, they want the holidays to be a time of peace and togetherness, not confrontation. But in their desire to preserve family traditions, they may unintentionally ask their children to set aside years of hurt that have never truly been resolved.

A second friend in her mid-thirties described how her once-close relationship with her brother deteriorated after years of conflict with his wife. What began as occasional disagreements gradually drove a deep wedge between them, culminating in an argument in which her brother accused her of being unfair to his wife and dismissed her attempts to explain why she felt hurt. The argument was never resolved, and neither sibling has made an effort to reconnect. Nearly three years later, they no longer exchange birthday wishes or speak on the phone, though their mother continues to invite them both home for the holidays, hoping they might finally put the past behind them.

She understands her mother’s longing for family togetherness and also mourns the bond she once shared with her brother. This friend says she resents the expectation that she should set aside years of unresolved hurt to preserve the illusion of family harmony.

Of course, not all siblings who have grown apart stop speaking entirely. Some continue to exchange birthday cards, send presents to each other's children, and share holiday meals. But beneath those gestures of goodwill, the relationship may have become more about honoring a shared past than maintaining a connection in the present. These rituals may be a way of holding on to what remains when neither person quite knows how to bridge the distance between them.

Another friend who is about the same age described a different kind of sibling distance, one rooted not in conflict but in a lack of closeness. She and her older sister never shared the kind of bond that made them confidantes growing up. Now living in different states, they keep in touch sporadically and see each other at family events, but rarely try to connect beyond those occasions.

This third friend has made peace with the fact that she and her sister are fundamentally different people who might never have become friends had they not been related. While she cherishes her relationship with her nephews, she no longer believes that being sisters obliges them to be close.

There can be freedom in accepting a relationship for what it is rather than what we think it ought to be. Not every strained sibling relationship requires a difficult conversation or a reckoning with the past. Sometimes people can acknowledge their differences, adjust their expectations, and move forward.

But when years of resentment have accumulated, trust has been broken, or siblings remember the same childhood very differently, making peace may require more than simply agreeing to leave the past behind.

We can spend years examining our behavior, confronting old wounds, and learning how to build healthier relationships. But what happens when the person we're trying to make peace with has no interest in doing the same? Even an offer to attend counseling together can go unanswered, leaving one sibling wondering whether reconciliation is possible when the other isn't willing to participate.

Ultimately, we can take responsibility for our own mistakes, offer forgiveness, and leave the door open to reconciliation. But we cannot make someone else walk through it.

Of course, family relationships are different from romantic ones. They are woven into the stories of who we are, the homes we grew up in, the parents who raised us, and the children who come after us. Creating distance from a sibling can mean losing far more than one relationship. It can mean missing a niece's birthday party, learning about a nephew's first day of school secondhand, or realizing you've become a stranger to children you once held as babies. Weddings become occasions for carefully arranged seating, and family celebrations become reminders of who's missing rather than opportunities to enjoy being together.

Acknowledging these losses doesn't mean every fractured relationship can or should be repaired. But it does raise an important question: How do we continue to love our families without asking one another to ignore the realities of those relationships?

The first step may be accepting that loving your family doesn't mean agreeing to every expectation that comes with being part of it. For some, that means attending Thanksgiving dinner but choosing not to stay overnight. For others, it means celebrating Christmas with their parents on a different day to avoid a strained sibling relationship, or declining a family gathering without being made to feel guilty. It may also mean maintaining a loving relationship with their parents without being expected to reconcile with a sibling.

Rather than insisting that everyone celebrate together, families can ask what each person feels comfortable with, respect those boundaries, and find new ways to spend time together. The goal doesn't have to be recreating the holidays we remember. It can be making room for the family we are today, rather than the one we wish we still were.

Maybe the greatest gift we can give one another this holiday season isn't another wrapped present or another carefully staged family photograph. Maybe it's the freedom to acknowledge that our relationships are complicated, that love doesn't erase years of hurt, and that sharing a holiday table isn't the same as sharing a close relationship.

Because sometimes the hardest part of going home for the holidays isn't facing the people we've grown apart from.

It's pretending we haven't grown apart.

item.title: A Guide to the 4 Caucuses That Could Shape the Democratic House
item.description: From the centrists to the progressives, here's how the key caucuses compare in size and membership

media:content.media:description: Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the Speaker-designate, speaks alongside two other House Democratic leaders, Representatives Katherine Clark and Pete Aguilar, on Nov. 18, 2026, during a news conference at the Capitol in Washington, DC.

item.content:encoded:
Democrats are preparing to take control of the House of Representatives with a substantially larger majority and an influx of new members who cover every corner of the party’s “big tent.” 


Incoming Democratic freshman include several democratic socialists and even more moderates who won in competitive and Republican-leaning districts. Many campaigned on lowering costs, improving health care, and providing a practical alternative to President Donald Trump. Some promised to fight for more sweeping changes to the country's economic and political systems.

The competing priorities will be among the biggest challenges for Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the speaker-designate, who will be tasked with maintaining unity in a party whose leaders frequently celebrate its ideological diversity. 

Much of that debate will unfold within the House's major ideological and governing caucuses, which are preparing to welcome dozens of new members when Congress convenes in January.
The two heavyweights are the centrist New Democrat Coalition—the largest caucus—and the Congressional Progressive Caucus, but the smaller Blue Dog Coalition and the bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus could also prove influential as Democrats confront the limits of what they can accomplish with Trump in the White House and a Senate where most major legislation will still require Republican support.

The new members will not necessarily divide neatly along ideological lines, and membership in the groups can overlap. But their growing ranks offer an early indication of where lawmakers may seek allies and how the party's internal balance of power could change. 

Here are the four caucuses to watch in the next Congress.

New Democrat Coalition

Estimated membership: 142 House Democrats

Overview: With over 140 members, the New Democrat Coalition is not only the largest Democratic caucus, it is poised to represent more than half of the Democrats in the House. Its members, who sit at the party's center, generally favor pragmatic economic policies, private-sector growth and bipartisan compromise. Its expansion reflects the importance of moderate candidates to Democrats' electoral success in November.

The coalition's growing membership could give it considerable influence over which bills reach the House floor, particularly as Jeffries seeks to demonstrate that the new Democratic majority can deliver results on the economic concerns that dominated the midterm campaign. Many of its incoming members represent competitive districts where voters may be skeptical of more expansive progressive proposals, giving them a strong political incentive to focus on measures that can attract broader support.

Members in the new Congress: The coalition added 40 members, including about 30 Democrats who flipped Republican-held seats in the midterms. Its new members include Representatives-elect Amish Shah and JoAnna Mendoza of Arizona; Richard Pan, Jacqui Irwin, and Marni von Wilpert of California; Jessica Killin and Manny Rutinel of Colorado; Luke Bronin of Connecticut; Pia Dandiya of Florida; Christina Bohannan, Lindsay James, and Sarah Trone Garriott of Iowa; Donna Miller and Melissa Bean of Illinois; J.D. Ford of Indiana; Zach Dembo of Kentucky; Adrian Boafo of Maryland; Sean McCann, Christina Hines, and Jeremy Moss of Michigan; Jake Johnson of Minnesota; Fred Wellman of Missouri; Jamie Ager of North Carolina; Denise Powell of Nebraska; Stefany Shaheen of New Hampshire; Rebecca Bennett of New Jersey; Teresa Benitez-Thompson of Nevada; Cait Conley of New York; Kristina Knickerbocker of Ohio; Bob Harvie, Paige Cognetti, and Janelle Stelson of Pennsylvania; Nancy Lacore of South Carolina; Bobby Pulido and Johnny Garcia of Texas; Ben McAdams of Utah; Shannon Taylor and Elaine Luria of Virginia; and Mitchell Berman and Rebecca Cooke of Wisconsin.

Leadership: Representative Nikki Budzinski of Illinois was elected as chairman for the next Congress. Other leaders include Representatives Gabe Vasquez of New Mexico, Kim Schrier of Washington, Greg Landsman of Ohio and Marilyn Strickland of Washington as vice chairs.

Policy priorities: The group outlined its legislative ambitions in an Affordability Agenda released in February, which focuses on five major household expenses: health care, housing, energy, family care and everyday essentials such as groceries. Its proposals include extending Affordable Care Act tax credits, strengthening Medicare and Medicaid, restricting surprise medical billing and expanding prescription drug price protections. On housing, the coalition wants to ease permitting and zoning restrictions to help build four million new homes over the next decade. It has also called for a national paid family and medical leave program, expanded access to universal prekindergarten and measures to increase competition in the grocery industry.

The coalition has placed particular emphasis on reversing Trump's tariffs, which its members argue have increased costs for consumers and businesses. Its agenda also calls for restoring congressional authority over trade policy and making it easier to build new energy infrastructure, including through changes to federal permitting requirements.

What to watch: The coalition's influence could prove especially significant in debates over health care, where some moderates favor expanding existing programs rather than pursuing Medicare for All, and in negotiations over which pieces of legislation stand a realistic chance of becoming law.

Congressional Progressive Caucus

Estimated membership: 105+ House Democrats

Overview: While the Squad gets more media attention, all of its members belong to the much larger Congressional Progressive Caucus, which more formally represents the party's left wing in the House. The CPC has long advocated policies including universal health care, stronger labor protections, immigration reform, climate action, and greater government intervention to address economic inequality. Jeffries, the Speaker-designate, is a former CPC member.

Members in the new Congress: Six newly elected Democrats who belong to the Democratic Socialists of America are expected to join: Representatives-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez of New York; Melat Kiros of Colorado; Angela Gonzales-Torres of California; Donavan McKinney of Michigan; and Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania. The caucus also announced that Daniel Biss (IL-9), Bob Brooks (PA-7), Sam Forstag (MT-1) and Patty Garcia (IL-4) have joined, and more could be added to its roster. 

Leadership: Representative Greg Casar of Texas serves as chairman, with Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota as deputy chair. Vice chairs include Representatives Ro Khanna of California and Rashida Tlaib of Michigan, and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York serves on the executive board. 

Policy priorities: In April, the CPC unveiled a 10-part New Affordability Agenda that would lower household expenses through a combination of expanded government benefits, tighter corporate regulation, and new restrictions on the influence of wealthy donors. Its proposals include capping child care expenses at 7% of family income, providing $20,000 in down payment assistance to first-time homebuyers, expanding rental assistance and creating a government program to sell discounted generic prescription drugs. Other proposals would require companies to pay double wages for overtime, guarantee workers two weeks of paid vacation, and prohibit businesses from using personal data and artificial intelligence to determine what prices it charges consumers. The agenda also calls for taxing excess profits earned by oil companies and returning the proceeds to consumers, restricting what the caucus considers excessive utility charges and abolishing super PACs.

What to watch: Although the caucus will remain smaller than the New Democrat Coalition, the arrival of newly elected democratic socialists could sharpen its demands of Democratic leadership. Several incoming lawmakers have already signaled that they intend to use their votes as leverage to secure commitments on issues like Medicare for All, defunding ICE, and ending American military assistance to Israel.

The breadth of the CPC’s agenda could create both opportunities for cooperation and points of friction with the party's moderate wing. Both the New Democrats and progressives have identified affordability as a top priority, and their proposals overlap on housing construction, prescription drug costs, and corporate competition. But the groups differ over how aggressively the federal government should intervene.

Blue Dog Coalition

Estimated membership: 23

Overview: The Blue Dogs describe themselves as fiscally responsible Democrats committed to practical economic policies, national security, and the needs of communities that are sometimes overlooked by national party leaders, including rural and tribal areas. Once a major force in the party, the Blue Dogs are now one of the smallest ideological groups in the House.

 

Members in the new Congress: The new class of Blue Dog Democrats includes Representatives-elect Johnny Garcia and Bobby Pulido of Texas, JoAnna Mendoza of Arizona, Jamie Ager and Paul Barringer of North Carolina, Sam Forstag of Montana, Rebecca Cooke and Mitchell Berman of Wisconsin, Jake Johnson of Minnesota, Zach Dembo of Kentucky, Nancy Lacore of South Carolina, Bob Brooks of Pennsylvania, Zack Mullock of New Jersey, and Eileen Laubacher of Colorado. Many of the incoming members unseated Republican incumbents.

Leadership: The coalition is led by three co-chairs: Representatives Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington, Vicente Gonzalez of Texas, and Lou Correa of California. Representative Adam Gray of California will serve as Blue Dog PAC Chair.

Policy priorities: The Blue Dogs have traditionally emphasized fiscal discipline, government accountability, and a willingness to break with party leadership on issues important to their districts.

What to watch: The Blue Dogs could become important voices in negotiations over federal spending, particularly if Democratic leaders seek Republican support for legislation. They could also exert influence over the party's political messaging, arguing that retaining control of the House in 2028 will depend on demonstrating that Democrats can govern effectively in districts where conservative voters remain a substantial part of the electorate.

Bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus

Estimated membership: Unknown. In the last Congress, it included 23 Democrats and 20 Republicans.

Overview: Unlike the other three groups, the Problem Solvers Caucus is explicitly bipartisan, bringing together moderate Democrats and Republicans who favor negotiation and compromise as a way to advance legislation in an increasingly polarized Congress.

Members in the new Congress: The caucus does not endorse candidates because of its bipartisan structure, and a list of incoming members has not been announced. Democrats retained 19 seats held by caucus members in the midterms, while Republicans lost 13 seats represented by members of the group.

Leadership: Unknown. The past chairs were Representatives Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, a Republican who lost his seat, and Tom Suozzi, a Democrat who won re-election. 

Policy priorities: The caucus describes its mission as building relationships across party lines and identifying areas of agreement on major policy questions. Its members have generally sought to position themselves as pragmatic lawmakers willing to negotiate with the opposing party, even when doing so invites criticism from their own political bases. 

What to watch: While Democrats will control both chambers of Congress next year, Trump will remain in the White House, so any measure that reaches the President's desk will be subject to his veto. Most major bills will also still need Republican support to overcome the Senate filibuster. The Problem Solvers Caucus could play an important role in bridging those divides, particularly on issues such as health care and government funding.

item.title: An Ode to the Endeavour Space Shuttle
item.description: "Though it will live now as a static, displayed part of space history, Endeavor is, nonetheless, still breathtaking," writes Marsha Ivins.

media:content.media:credit: Myung J. Chun—Los Angeles Times/Getty Images
media:content.media:description: Space Shuttle Endeavour in its launch position at the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center at the California Science Center on Nov. 13, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
I’m standing on the floor of the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center of the California Science Center under the tail of the new exhibit of the Space Shuttle Endeavour and remembering how I felt looking up at that same shuttle on the launch pad at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida. There is no one word to describe that feeling: wonder, awe, amazement, immense pride that we could build and fly such a machine. How was this my job, I think to myself.

I’d spent a large part of my NASA career as an astronaut supporting shuttle missions at the Kennedy Space Center; testing the vehicles about to fly; packing equipment bags for flight; sitting in a shuttle on the launch pad before the tank was fueled; ensuring switches were in the right positions; even strapping crews in before launch. 

As an astronaut, I had the opportunity to be strapped in myself on five shuttle missions, two on Columbia, and three on Atlantis. And for the decade prior to being selected into the astronaut office in 1984, I worked as an engineer at the Johnson Space Center on the development of this very spacecraft. Suffice it to say space was my jam and Shuttle my focus. 

Before a launch, the support structure is rolled away, and the shuttle stands alone, illuminated in bright lights. Everyone, save the handful of closeout and flight crew, is moved to 5 miles away. The vehicle sits fueled and alive, releasing small clouds of condensation from the tanks of cryogenic propellant, the epitome of potential energy. There is a quiet, intense anticipatory charge to the atmosphere. 

Standing now at the base of a stacked space shuttle in a museum, I am still moved by this extraordinary embodiment of technical audacity.  

The story of the Space Shuttle often seems like an abbreviated footnote in NASA’s history, homage still paid to the Apollo program. Interest is now focused on the anticipated return of Americans to the moon with the Artemis Program. Authorized in the 1970’s after Nixon canceled the Apollo program, the Space Shuttle was the world’s first reusable spacecraft, with all major components except the external fuel tank designed to be recovered and reused. It was billed at the time as taking spaceflight into the everyday realm of air travel, allowing access to orbit for all commercial, scientific, and military payloads.

The contract for four flight vehicles and one atmospheric test vehicle went to the company Rockwell (now Boeing) in 1972. In 1977, that test vehicle, Enterprise, made its first of five free-flying approach and landing tests from the back of a 747, to demonstrate that a 200-ton glider with the aerodynamic performance of a cinder block could, in fact, be safely, successfully, and repeatedly landed on a conventional runway. In 1981, the first of the orbital shuttles, Columbia, made its maiden flight, flying 28 missions until its tragic accident during reentry in 2003.

Challenger, the second shuttle to be built, made its first flight in 1983 and was lost on ascent during its 10th flight in 1986. The third vehicle, Discovery, launched in 1984, completed a record 39 missions before its final flight in 2011. The fourth vehicle, Atlantis, launched in 1985, completed 33 missions, ending the Shuttle program with its final mission in 2011. 

And then there was Endeavour. Born as a replacement for Challenger in 1987 and built largely from structural spare parts delivered as part of the original contract, Endeavour made her maiden flight in 1992, flying 25 missions, retiring in 2011. At the end of the shuttle program, after 135 flights, the decision was made to send the remaining orbital shuttles to museums and display them in the three flight configurations. Discovery rests on the ground in landing configuration at the Udvar-Hazy Center of the Smithsonian Air and Space Museum. Atlantis hangs in the Kennedy Space Center Visitor’s Complex in glorious flight configuration. 

And finally, Endeavour in launch configuration is now housed in a dedicated building, itself a structural work of art. The spacecraft rests on the last external tank built and two flight solid rocket boosters. And though it will live now as a static displayed part of space history, Endeavor is, nonetheless, still breathtaking. Seen from one angle as you enter the room, it sits in full pre-launch glory. Seen from another angle, one payload bay door open, the insulation material and the structure underneath can be seen. Ride the glass elevator to the very top, and you can see the view looking down on the entire stack, a view only those people working on the launch pad can typically see. 

It was at the base of the display, standing a hand's distance from the tip of the tail, looking up at this impossible realization of 35 years of Shuttle history, that I realized the lump in my throat had not dissolved for my entire tour.  

Where once she stood on the launch pad eager to fly, Endeavour stands now forever static, potential energy forever spent. But she remains an inspiration for ingenuity and determination; a tribute to those audacious ideas made reality, and to the technical firsts in human spaceflight. She still demands respect and humbling appreciation for the thousands of people in the NASA and contractor workforce whose minds and hands got those of us who flew to the pointy end. She serves as a living memorial to the hearts and souls of lives lived and lost. And now Endeavour, along with Discovery and Atlantis, lives on as a reminder of a capability in human spaceflight we no longer have.

item.title: How the War Turned Sudan Into a Country Without a Newspaper
item.description: Thirty four journalists have been killed in Sudan since the war erupted. Yet Sudanese journalists continue to take great risks to gather credible information.

media:content.media:description: Ahmed Aman, a Sudanese man, who spoke about being imprisoned and tortured in Rapid Support Forces' prisons before fleeing El-Fasher, sits at a makeshift shelter in the town of Tawila Sudan's Darfur region on March 2, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
A war of narratives is being waged within the war in Sudan. The warring parties—the official Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary force—are fighting an information war through traditional and social media. Misinformation, disinformation, hate speech, and propaganda are routinely deployed, and Sudanese journalists have become targets. 

Thirty-four journalists have been killed in Sudan in the past three and a half years of war. Sixteen of them are believed to have been targeted for their journalistic work. Hundreds of journalists have been displaced with their families and lost their jobs; dozens have been threatened, assaulted, and detained. Most of the Sudanese newspaper offices, television studios and radio stations have been looted, damaged, or destroyed.

For the first time in over a century, Sudan has gone without a single newspaper being printed in more than three years. Yet Sudanese journalists have worked hard to inform the world of the costs of the war in their country: more than 400,000 people are estimated to have been killed; 12 million are believed to have been displaced; widespread destruction, looting, hunger, and human rights abuses have ravaged the African nation of 53 million people.

The war has effectively divided Sudan into two zones of control: the SAF holding around 60% of the territory concentrating in eastern and central Sudan, and the RSF controlling about 40% of the country concentrating in Darfur and adjoining areas in southern and western Sudan. Both the SAF and the RSF maintain a tight control over what can be reported from the areas they control.

The New York Times reported that SAF used banned chemical weapons in the war, and a UN fact-finding report accused the RSF of sexual violence and slavery and described its violence in El- Fasher as bearing the “defining characteristics of genocide."

Seeking credible information from the ground has turned Sudanese journalists into targets. In July, the Sudanese Journalists Syndicate (SJS) and the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) submitted a report to the U.N. Human Rights Council on the regression of press freedom and the intimidation of journalists during the war in Sudan. “The war came with a knockout punch to the press,” recalled Abdelmonium Abouedries, a veteran journalist and chairman of the SJS. “Truth became the war’s first victim.” 

A heroic reporter in El-Fasher

On Oct. 10, 2023, Halima Idris Salim, a correspondent for Sudan Bukra, an independent non-profit media platform, was reporting on the dire conditions of a hospital in the city of Omdurman, northwest of the capital Khartoum. An RSF vehicle ran over her on a street and killed her.

The Sudanese army wasn't innocent either. In December 2024, the SAF arrested Yahya Hamad Fadlallah and his son at their home in Khartoum. An editor, columnist, and novelist, Fadlallah was celebrated for his novel Zugendi’s Marriage in Sudan. According to the SJS and Darfur Bar Association, he was falsely accused of collaborating with the RSF, tortured, and denied treatment for diabetes in detention. After being released on Jan. 10, 2025, Fadlallah was admitted to a hospital, but died there three days later. 

Apart from the killings, Sudanese journalists have faced threats and criminal charges for their work. In May, Rishan Oshi, a journalist with AlBalad TV, a private television network, was sentenced to a year in prison and fined $16,553 for defamation by a court in Port Sudan. The charges against her were filed after she posted an article about government corruption on her popular Facebook page.

The costs of reporting on active hostilities can be dangerously high. In April 2025, the Sudanese military took back control of Khartoum, but the war intensified in the Darfur region. The RSF had besieged the city of El Fashir in Darfur to consolidate their control over the region.

Mouammar Ibrahim, a freelance reporter for Al Jazeera Mubashir, reported on the long siege and the terrible human conditions in the city. The RSF shelled and attacked the city with drones, enforced starvation and blocked aid. Some people survived on animal feed. A famine stalked El-Fashir and its displaced people, living in camps nearby.

Days before the fall of El-Fashir in Oct. 2025, Ibrahim tried to leave the city with thousands of others. The RSF fighters identified, abducted, and detained him. The paramilitary force proceeded to kill, detain, and disappear thousands as it captured the city. In a social media video, the RSF authorities claimed that they were investigating Ibrahim's "biased" reporting and that he would face a trial. "The journalist is a victim of arbitrary detention,” said Martin Roux of Reporters Without Borders, “held in conditions that pose a grave threat to his life.”

Honoring bravehearts

Yet despite these grave difficulties, Sudanese journalists have carried on reporting on the war and other political and social stories that continue to affect lives in their country and earned well-deserved recognition for their bravery. Salma Abdel Aziz, an independent journalist, reported on the imprisonment and murder of violence young girls and women by their families in Darfur for possessing mobile phones. Her reporting won her the Intergovernmental Authority on Development Media Award.

Zeinab Mohammed Salih, an independent journalist, reported on the eruption of war from Khartoum for The Guardian, The Financial Times, and the BBC. She was the first journalist to report and verify the 2023 Geneina massacres in Darfur, where thousands were killed. She also reported from El-Fasher before its fall. Salih was awarded the 2026 ICJF Knight International Journalism Award.

In the chaotic opening weeks of the war, AlMidgad Hassan, a pharmacology graduate with some media training, started reporting for Alhadath, an Arabic news network, which is part of the Saudi Al Arabiya network. His first report was from inside a bombed apartment in Khartoum using a smart phone held by a friend. He continued to report for Alhadath for three years, often seen in a helmet and flak jacket around war-torn Khartoum. For his work, he was awarded the 2026 Press Freedom Unlimited Newcomer of the Year Award. In 2026, he moved on to work for Aljazeera English.

Four stories of Sudan won at the 2026 One World Media Awards in London, which honors reporting on the Global South. Mohammed Amin, a Sudanese journalist won One World Media’s Journalist of the Year Award for his reporting on how villagers in central Sudan defended themselves against the RSF. But Amin was denied a visa to the United Kingdom to receive his prize. “The Sudanese are not a heavy burden on this world but insisting to be equal partners in humanity,” he said in a video message.

Sudanese media groups were also recognized for their work during the war. Ayin Network, whose editors relocated to Kenya won the One World Media Press Freedom Award, as its reporters continued to report from Sudan publishing their work without bylines for their safety.

The Sudanese Journalists Syndicate, a journalist union, was awarded the 2026 UNESCO/Guillermo Cano World Press Freedom Prize Award for its work in highlighting the struggles of  Sudanese journalists, documenting attacks on the press, and defending Sudanese journalists. “I had nothing but tears,” Abouedries, the chairman of the SJS, told me, describing it as a moment of “pride and joy.” 

Awards alone cannot end Sudan’s war or the suffering of its people, but the attention, solidarity and commitment to truth they encourage can help. Silvia Chocarro, a senior strategic advisor to the International Press Institute (IPI) who lived in Sudan, told me, “When Sudanese journalists receive international recognition, there is a very powerful message: we see you, your work matters, and you are not alone.”

item.title: Big Tech Companies May Face Billion-Dollar Fines After Australia Passes ‘Digital Duty of Care’ Law
item.description: Tech firms may face fines in Australia of up to 5% of global revenue for failing to curb online harms on their platforms.
item.content:encoded:
Tech giants could face penalties of up to 5% of their global revenue if found in violation of new online safety rules in Australia.

The country’s Parliament passed the Digital Duty of Care bill Wednesday, Communications Minister Anika Wells said, after the center-left Labor Party government of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese reached a deal with the left-wing Greens party.

Australia has been a world pioneer in legislating protections against harms online. Last December, it implemented a global-first social media ban for residents under 16, which has had mixed results but has also inspired other countries to follow suit.

To Albanese, the Digital Duty of Care law is the next step. “It’s about Australia ‌taking ⁠action on the side of parents and children, not foreign-owned tech companies,” he told Parliament on Tuesday.

Tech firms like Meta and Apple, many of which are headquartered in the U.S., have said that they want to improve child protection and curb harm on their platforms, though they have pushed back against how broad they say Australia’s laws are. Critics of the Digital Duty of Care law particularly question who gets to decide what counts as harmful content.

David Brat, the U.S. Ambassador to Australia, said he had conveyed the Trump Administration’s objections to the law amendments to Wells on Tuesday.

“Vaguely defined ‘harms,’ backed by penalties of up to 5% of global revenue, will push platforms to censor lawful speech,” Brat posted on social media. “As Australia’s largest foreign investor, the U.S. is concerned with regulations that impose disproportionate compliance burdens on American companies relative to competitors.”

Last month, Wells told the National Press Club that the new law would apply to U.S. President Donald Trump’s Truth Social platform. On Tuesday, she said her ministry was ironing out differences with their American counterparts.

What does the Digital Duty of Care law do?

The law amends a collection of internet-related legislation, including Australia’s 2021 Online Safety Act, which set 17 online safety codes and standards to combat unlawful and age-restricted material. Amendments have been pursued for years amid criticisms that previous safeguards were inadequate. Wells said in October that those prior codes “were drafted by big tech for big tech.” 

The Digital Duty of Care law, which was introduced in Parliament in October, repeals those prior codes in favor of a broader “duty of care” requirement for tech firms, following a 12-month transition period. The duty mimics how Australia regulates other sectors, including aged care and child supervision, commercial vessel and rail safety, and workplace safety, in which businesses and providers are expected to manage risks to health and safety “as much as is reasonably practicable.” 

Under the Digital Duty of Care law, platforms must provide risk assessments to regulators at least once a year, and they must notify regulators before they introduce significant changes to their platforms that could allow for new risks of harm, such as “addictive” design features.

The amendments also make it easier for Australian citizens to hold tech companies to account. Previously, one needed to rely on complex legal avenues concerning company negligence and consumer protection. The new law grants Australians the “private right of action,” which means they can directly sue digital platforms for breaching their duty of care. 

The new law also implements stronger privacy protections for users, expanded regulatory powers to remove “nudifying” services, and a clarified definition of “hostile attitudes to women”—which now refers to material depicting hatred or the inferiority of women or promoting violence, abuse, exclusion, or the denial of women’s rights.The bill would also require tech firms to allow users in Australia to opt out of a platform’s algorithm and instead choose to see only content from accounts they follow. 

It also introduces steeper fines for violations, which Wells said the Australian public demanded. Initially, the proposed maximum penalty was 109 million Australian dollars ($72 million), but it was raised to up to 5% of the violator’s global revenue. The steep fines mirror those in other jurisdictions, including Canada’s proposed 3% penalty in a bill that would require Big Tech to reduce the risk of harmful content and the European Union’s draft 6% fine against companies that push for unfair trade practices.

How have critics responded?

The Tech Council of Australia, an industry body whose membership includes companies like Google, Microsoft, and LinkedIn, told the Guardian in a statement that it supported the legislation but was concerned over its impact on businesses, particularly in its empowering of individuals to sue.

“A private right of action is a complex undertaking with significant consequences,” a spokesperson said. “How this is implemented is critical, and we need proper consultation to ensure that businesses are not hindered from investing in Australia. If we get this wrong, it will be counterproductive to encouraging innovation in Australia.”

The conservative opposition coalition has called the law “a blank cheque for political censorship.” Senator Sarah Henderson said on Tuesday that the bill compromised current legislation, gave “extensive” powers to the government, and would hurt smaller tech businesses.

“The fact is the digital duty of care should never have seen the light of day,” Henderson said. “This is policy on the run, driven by an insidious agenda to shut down lawful speech and control political debate.”

Wells rejected this. “This is not about what you say online,” she said Wednesday. “It’s about what the platforms do or fail to do online.”

item.title: China’s Huawei Convicted in U.S. Over Bank Fraud, Iran Ties
item.description: China’s biggest technology firm and the world’s largest telecommunications equipment maker has been convicted in the U.S. of stealing trade secrets and defrauding banks about its business in Iran.
item.content:encoded:
China’s biggest technology firm and the world’s largest telecommunications equipment maker has been convicted in the U.S. of stealing trade secrets and defrauding banks about its business in Iran.

Huawei was found guilty on 10 of 12 counts by a jury in Brooklyn on Tuesday. The verdict all but brings to a close an almost eight-year-long criminal case against Huawei and three of its subsidiaries. The sprawling legal case spanned a 12-week trial, dozens of witnesses, and hundreds of motions and filings. 

It’s a rare case of U.S. prosecutors securing a conviction against a foreign corporation and could have significant consequences for both Huawei and U.S.-China relations. 

The Justice Department first announced charges against Huawei in January 2019 as part of the first-term Trump Administration’s “China Initiative,” a controversial program to investigate and prosecute Chinese influence and espionage in the U.S. 

The Shenzhen-based tech giant was found guilty of bank and wire fraud, conspiracy to steal trade secrets, and violations of U.S. sanctions. It faces massive potential penalties, including fines, forfeiture, and restitution. Sentencing is set for September 2027, with motions in advance of sentencing expected to start in the third week of January.

“Few crimes are as serious as Huawei’s decades-long pattern of endangering U.S. national security, violating the sanctity of U.S. commerce, and impeding the enforcement of U.S. laws,” U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. said.

James Barnacle Jr., assistant director in charge of the FBI’s New York office, added, “Huawei’s success was built on deception and theft, and the FBI will never hesitate to pursue those who profit by breaking the law.”

The jury, however, acquitted Huawei of the most serious charge: racketeering conspiracy under the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organisations Act (RICO).

Huawei’s attorney Brian Heberlig argued that U.S. prosecutors “began with guilt and worked backwards,” basing their claims of conspiracy on isolated incidents.

Huawei’s success, he said, is “about competition, not conspiracy. Innovation, not theft. Ordinary business dealings, not criminal conduct.”

Heberlig told reporters that the company will appeal the case.

“We believe the government’s remaining charges are equally without legal or factual merit,” Huawei said in a statement. “We will thoroughly review the relevant verdicts and take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests.”

Landmark convictions

Huawei was convicted of conspiracy to steal trade secrets from U.S. companies over two decades. Its alleged theft includes router source code from Cisco Systems, semiconductor equipment from CNEX Labs, robotic phone testing equipment from T-Mobile, antenna technology from Quintel, and networking equipment information from Fujitsu Network Communications. The jury also found Huawei and its subsidiaries guilty of violating the International Emergency Economic Powers Act and money laundering.

During the trial, which began Sept. 8, the jury watched a video that prosecutors said showed a Huawei engineer unbolting and detaching the arm of a high-speed T-Mobile testing robot and slipping it into his backpack. The engineer said he found the piece in his bag, calling the incident a “mistake,” and returned it the next day after T-Mobile reported it missing, but not before a visiting engineer from China allegedly measured and photographed the robotic arm, according to prosecutors. Huawei later fired the employee.

Prosecutors also argued that Huawei had hired a professor to gain access to a circuit board developed by CNEX.

“Huawei cultivated a culture of crime and corruption, and that crime was an important business strategy,” U.S. prosecutor Taylor Stout said in his opening statement.

Huawei’s attorneys called 15 witnesses to give evidence that the company’s success came from its own innovation. The attorneys cited the company’s 110,000-person research and development team and its over 165,000 patents. Heberlig said prosecutors had “cherry-picked” instances of employee misconduct that were not representative of Huawei’s company culture.

Prosecutors also argued that Huawei deliberately deceived global banks, including HSBC, BNP Paribas, and Standard Chartered, about its business in Iran and North Korea, which are both subject to U.S. sanctions. Huawei allegedly presented its Iran subsidiary, Skycom Tech, as an independent entity to skirt sanctions.

The jury, however, rejected the government’s assertion that Huawei had conspired in a racketeering scheme to expand its global business. If the company had been convicted of the RICO charge, it could have faced potential forfeiture of parts of its enterprise.

“It’s hard not to have profoundly mixed emotions from the verdict we just heard,” Heberlig, Huawei’s attorney, told reporters. The RICO charge, he said, “alleged that the company was corrupt from top to bottom, that it had a corporate culture and policy of cheating, stealing, and lying, and the jury found the company not guilty on that charge.”

The jury also acquitted the company of conspiring to obstruct a federal grand jury investigation.

The legal case is among the most extensive against a corporation, involving millions of documents in evidence, covering source code, financial records, and emails. Jurors spent five days, beginning Nov. 18, deliberating the case.

“Rarely has a jury had to commit so much of their personal time to a trial,” U.S. District Judge Ann Donnelly, who oversaw the case, said.

The case also took a winding path before the trial even began. It was delayed for years during the COVID-19 pandemic. In 2022, U.S. prosecutors also charged two Chinese intelligence officers with trying to bribe a U.S. government employee with $61,000 in bitcoin to steal evidence and information about the case.

U.S.-China relations

The case could have ramifications on the U.S.’s relationship with China. The verdict comes days after President Donald Trump met with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen. It also comes amid tensions over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy, which has renewed calls by U.S. lawmakers for tighter restrictions on A.I. chip sales to China.

Huawei, which is privately held, is one of China’s largest and most famous companies. The company reported 880.9 billion RMB ($126 billion) in revenue last year. It employs more than 200,000 employees globally and operates in more than 170 countries.

The case spawned a diplomatic crisis in 2018, when Canadian authorities detained Huawei Chief Financial Officer Meng Wanzhou, who is also the daughter of the company’s founder, at the U.S.’s request. Meng had been secretly indicted on U.S. charges of bank and wire fraud.

Meng pleaded not guilty to criminal charges and fought extradition to the U.S. while under house arrest in Vancouver for nearly three years. She entered a deferred prosecution agreement in 2021, which acknowledged that she had misled an HSBC banker about Huawei’s relationship with Skycom, after which she returned to China. A federal judge dismissed the charges against her with prejudice in December 2022. The HSBC executive Meng had met with in 2013 testified in the Brooklyn trial.

The first charges were announced as Washington and Beijing were locked in a trade war.

Since the first-term Trump Administration launched the “China Initiative” in 2018, federal prosecutors have secured convictions against a number of foreign nationals, but corporate cases have had mixed outcomes. Taiwan’s United Microelectronics pleaded guilty to stealing trade secrets in 2020, and China’s Hytera Communications pleaded guilty to conspiring to steal trade secrets in 2025. Chinese chipmaker Fujian Jinhua was acquitted in 2024. A separate federal case in Seattle against two Huawei subsidiaries has been repeatedly delayed, with a trial date set for October 2027. The Justice Department ended the initiative in 2022 after criticism that it unfairly targeted academics and researchers of Chinese descent.

Months after announcing the charges against Huawei in 2019, the Trump Administration placed Huawei on a Commerce Department blacklist over national security concerns.

China’s foreign ministry has repeatedly criticized the prosecution as politically motivated and an effort to suppress Chinese companies. The Chinese government has said the “China Initiative” and other actions by the Trump Administration, both first- and second-term, used national security as a pretext to contain China.

“The Chinese government firmly opposes the U.S. side’s suppression and containment of Chinese enterprises,” foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said in September. “China firmly supports Chinese enterprises in safeguarding their legitimate rights and interests.”

item.title: Ariana Grande Is the Saving Grace of the Woefully Unfunny Focker In-Law
item.description: In an era of reboots and sequels, the return of the Fockers was inevitable. At least Ariana Grande has joined to lighten up the proceedings

media:content.media:description: Ben Stiller and Ariana Grande in Focker In-Law

item.content:encoded:
Though it may seem like only yesterday, the last Fockers film appeared 16 years ago, which means enough time has passed for little Fockers to become big ones and older Fockers to face the same challenge their Forefockers had to tackle the first time around, in 2000’s Meet the Parents. What if you meet your offspring’s new squeeze and find him or her wanting? That’s where Ben Stiller’s Greg Focker finds himself in Focker In-Law, the fourth installment in a series that seemed to have found its natural end with 2010’s Little Fockers. Then again, in an era of reboots and rehashes, any franchise can be resurrected. More Focking around was inevitable, and your enjoyment of Focker In-Law will depend on your tolerance for Stiller’s particular brand of sharp-edged self-pity, as well as Robert De Niro’s penchant for squinting and mugging through a scene—although, at least, Ariana Grande has arrived on the scene. Underestimate her at your peril.

This time around Greg and Pam Focker—the latter again played by Teri Polo—return to Pam’s homestead, where her judgmental ex-CIA father, De Niro’s Jack Byrnes, waits to torment his ever-disappointing son-in-law. Greg and Pam’s grown children, Henry (Skyler Gisondo, secret MVP of the recent Primetime) and Samantha (Beanie Feldstein), will also be visiting, their respective significant others in tow: Samantha’s boyfriend is Eduardo (Eduardo Franco, of Booksmart and Stranger Things ), a polite, likable guy who nevertheless has some boundary issues. (After using the master bathroom at the Fockers’ house, he announces amiably that he’s commandeered Pam’s razor to beautify his private parts.) And sweet, somewhat shy Henry, a med student, has landed a beautiful and totally together girlfriend, Grande's Olivia. En route to the family reuinion—it’s Jack’s 80th birthday, and there’s a huge bash planned—Greg meets Olivia without knowing who she is: She’s in the first class cabin of their flight, and he’s in the back with the rest of the "unwashed.”  Desperate to use the bathroom, he makes his way up the aisle and into the forbidden zone; a wildly unfunny encounter ensues, during which he steals, for no discernible reason, Olivia’s birth-control pills. She catches him in the act, writing him off as a creep, not knowing he’s her boyfriend’s father.

From there, the failed jokes pile up like dead leaves. Jack, historically a traditional meat-and-potatoes guy, has gone on a health kick and become vegan. Greg, eager to impress him, has planned a big steak dinner and refuses to pivot, so Olivia steps in to prepare an elaborate and delicious meatless meal. Meanwhile, Greg sears his eyebrows off while overcooking a big pile of meat that proves to be inedible. If the old overcooked-steak gag doesn’t do it for you, there’s so much more: Jack has adopted a German Shepherd who likes everybody but Greg. (Jack speaks to the dog in German; Greg insists the dog is anti-Semitic.) Though everyone in the family, especially Jack, adores Olivia, Greg doesn’t trust her, and does everything he can to sabotage her relationship with his son. His misplaced aggression is supposed to be hilarious. Somehow, it’s assumed that we’ll feel sympathy for poor, unlikable Greg, who means well but is forced to suffer one humiliation after another. De Niro’s Jack may be a cartoony hard ass, but at least his character has some shape and heft. Greg is just a jerk, and to see Stiller’s eyes desperately pleading for our likes is about as far from funny as you can get.

But at least there’s Grande, whose superb timing brings some lightness to the proceedings, even as Stiller and De Niro chomp down hard on every gag. Focker In-Law was directed by John Hamburg, who also cowrote the script; his writing credits include the other Focker movies as well. It’s hard to say why, exactly, Focker In-Law is so dismal; maybe it’s just the kind of unholy brew you get when you jumble together mediocre direction, a lackluster script, and performers who are trying way too hard. But Grande singlehandedly salvages whole sections of the movie. Her Olivia is an executive coach, but that’s a fairly new endeavor. She was formerly, she reveals brightly, an F.B.I. hostage negotiator—and when she drops this bit of information, batting her Bambi eyelashes, it’s as if the comedy gods had seen our suffering and deigned to offer us a respite. Olivia is a chipper overachiever, the kind of young woman we, like Greg, might naturally distrust. But Grande takes our eagerness to pre-judge and ties it into a great big taffeta bow. Before we know it, we wish we had a friend like Olivia, a woman who’s not only good at what she does, but who also shows kindness and a higher-than-necessary tolerance for the idiots around her. You’ll need similar fortitude to survive Focker In-Law, but at least she proves it can be done.

item.title: How AI Is Changing What Companies Know About Their Customers
item.description: AI is making consumer data more valuable to businesses—with new implications for personal privacy.

media:content.media:credit: Photo-Illustration by Chloe Dowling for TIME (Source Images: TGI/Tetra Images/Getty Images, Duncan_Andison/Getty Images)

item.content:encoded:
Fifteen years ago, when he worked as an adviser to the pharmaceutical industry, Jeff Gaus’ firm bought drugstore cash-register data. From those records, he says, the company could tell pharma reps that, for example, “Dr. Smith has three people with this condition” and instruct them to go pitch their wares to that doctor.

That felt cutting edge, but it’s nothing compared to what Gaus has seen recently. What took multiple days and several number-crunching humans to figure out back then can be worked out in minutes or seconds by artificial intelligence, he says. using mammoth amounts of customer data and other personal information from an ever-expanding universe of sources to narrowcast advertising, often down to the individual level.

“A friend of mine who used to be a CEO of a retail organization, his saying was, ‘Retail is detail,’” Gaus says. “The more I know about you, the better off I can sell to you." 

Indeed, information about medical purchases is just one example. Social media users receive certain toy or book recommendations that appear to be based on photos or videos they’ve posted of their children reading or playing with something similar. People who have searched airline prices for certain dates to specific destinations may notice matching promotions from tour companies. And now, online shoppers have the experience of searching for something or asking a chatbot a question and, within minutes or hours, being served with uncannily precise advertising messages. 

Targeted marketing is not new. But AI has dramatically ramped up the speed and intensity of the longstanding race to know one’s customer. Even without more sophisticated systems, AI is reshaping how many companies think about customer data simply because of the sheer volume of information it can process. Some systems go as far as creating constantly evolving “digital twin” models of specific people or small populations to predict consumer behavior based on a matrix of financial and personal data points.

This vast amount of information is not limited to just purchases,  but also the data millions of people have been giving away for decades in the form of opinions, preferences, personal stories, geolocations, photos, and videos in search engines and on social-media platforms.

All that information exists online for companies to process, now that AI can make it more useful and less overwhelming , says Justin Sherman, founder of Duke University’s Privacy and Democracy Project and author of a forthcoming book on the data-broker industry titled The Middlemen. 

“For a person or a company to process the amount of data that AI collects would require lots of manpower and a lot of time—and you'd have systems in place to decide how to sort it and what you're going do with it,” echoes Callie Schroeder, director of the AI and Human Rights Program at the Electronic Privacy Information Center. “Those factors don't really come into play with AI because it is able to go through that information so fast and sort and parse out what it is it wants to pull from it.”

For privacy advocates like Schroeder, these practices raise important red flags about data ownership. Part of the reason this material is useful, Sherman points out, is that AI is able to draw information that is specific enough to be commercially beneficial out of even anonymized records. This, too, isn’t new; in 2009, Ars Technica wrote about how data scientists had shown they could “re-identify” sets of supposedly anonymized information—from medical records to AOL searches—with remarkable ease. That piece was based on research by Georgetown University law professor Paul Ohm who is quoted as saying, “Data can either be useful or perfectly anonymous, but never both.”

But as with so many realms of digital life, the speed with which this is possible today is orders of magnitude faster.

“It's easier for these AI-advertising technology companies and data brokers to mash it all together and link it back to people,” says Sherman, now CEO of Global Cyber Strategies. “A company or a research organization or consumer might share information thinking that it's quote-unquote anonymized.”

But controlling one’s own data and how it’s used can be complicated and laborious even for the most tech-savvy.

“I just got a new phone and I had to manually go through all of those settings and turn off a whole bunch of machine-learning things. I was looking up what each of those things meant. It's a lot of work and it's unfair that we have to do it,” Shroeder says, arguing that it would be better for society if laws and norms caught up to the need for a shared approach to what consumers should be able to expect.

Of course, the trade-off for consumers in any given moment is convenience—which may make them less likely to closely monitor those settings.  

“I bought plenty of things through targeted ads I've gotten online, right? So it's not that it doesn't work,” says Sherman, who cites the recommendations on music and video streaming services as something that he has particularly appreciated. The thing to watch out for, in his view, is a situation in which consumers aren’t offered a meaningful way to give or withdraw consent for use of their personal data. 

Gaus, now CEO of the Provenance Chain Group, which provides technological infrastructure for supply-chain planning, points to how retailers decide which goods to keep stocked in which warehouses for the fastest delivery. They use purchase patterns, yes, but also other granular data gleaned off credit-card charges, AI chatbot inquiries, even voting patterns to understand product preferences down to specific ZIP codes.

 

“How do they know to have certain products pre-positioned that I can get delivered the same day?” he says. “It's because they've studied consumption patterns and have profiled populations and know with a really high probability that this is going to get purchased by somebody nearby in some period of time.”

Gaus says the depth and breadth of data available sometimes surprises even him. He appeared on a panel about data use in the supply chain earlier this year, he recalls, during which a fellow panelist who had formerly been in the government intelligence sector recounted meetings he had had in Silicon Valley during which he’d asked what information a tech company could access about a person.“He showed us a map,” Gaus recalls the panelist saying, “where he was able to plot all of [this person’s] consumer purchases on all of his credit cards over the last 45 days, where his car had driven, what telephone calls he'd been making, off data that is collected by private corporations.”

 

And the specificity of what companies are able to know about their customers is only going to get more astounding, Gaus says.

“Let me put it this way: If you put it on a scale of one to 10, one being ‘I have no knowledge of you’ and 10 being ‘I've got almost perfect knowledge of you,’ I would say that five years ago we were maybe at a five or a six,” he says. “Today, I think we're at like 9.2, 9.3, something like that. If I have access to and am willing to, I can acquire pretty much any data that I need about you.”
