item.title: ‘They Never Stop’: Taipei Mayoral Candidate Puma Shen on Fighting Chinese Cognitive Warfare
item.description: Puma Shen tells TIME how stronger community ties and a thriving tech sector can help Taipei prosper and prepare for threats from China

media:group.media:description: The southern Taiwanese city of Chiayi has long been synonymous with a cherished culinary staple: turkey rice, served drenched in savory soy broth and topped with lard-fried shallots and pickled radish. Introduced by American GIs after World War II, the non-native bird became an affordable alternative to chicken and quickly became a local icon. Eight decades later, Chiayi is anchoring its identity in a very different military legacy: uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs). Today, more than 50 companies and research institutions have set up shop nearby, transforming the county into Taiwan’s premier drone hub.

item.content:encoded:
The legislative office of Puma Shen feels more like a college dorm than a lawmaker’s workplace. Every surface is piled high with anime figurines, camping equipment, and baseball memorabilia. “I don’t have enough space at home, so I have to put it all in my office,” he tells TIME. “Otherwise, my wife will be p—d off!”

Read more: How Taiwan Is Turning Tech Supremacy Into a Security Shield

Then the décor turns political. A large Ukrainian flag, signed by troops during Shen’s 2023 visit, hangs on one wall. On the door, a piece of Chinese calligraphy reads “Die-hard Taiwanese independence separatist”—a designation Beijing applied to him that has become a point of pride. “On the first day when I was sanctioned by China, my colleague actually gave this to me,” grins Shen, 44.

It’s a sanction that illustrates Shen’s position in Taiwan politics, where fault lines are increasingly drawn between competing visions for preserving the self-ruling island’s autonomy. Beijing claims sovereignty over Taiwan and has not ruled out using force to achieve “reunification.” Shen’s ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) sees security in forging a path distinct from Beijing; the opposition Nationalists (KMT), meanwhile, believe building bridges with China better serves the islanders' interests.

On Nov. 28, Taiwan is holding local elections that will serve as a bellwether of the national mood, and Shen is hoping to unseat the KMT incumbent Chiang Wan-an for the prestigious post of Taipei mayor, often a steppingstone to the presidency. 

Besides serving as a lawmaker, Shen is also an associate professor of criminology at National Taipei University and in 2019 co-founded Doublethink Lab, a civil society research group that tracks disinformation, cognitive warfare, and digital authoritarianism. 

The following has been edited for clarity and length.

TIME: You're standing as the DPP candidate for Taipei mayor. What is the number one problem Taipei faces that you want to fix?

City-level issues, for instance, like transportation, or making sure that streets are clean, [are important]. But I also care about resilience, I care about prosperity, and I think prosperity and resilience are actually the same thing, because the city can only be prosperous in the long run if it can hold together when anything happens.

So it's not just about infrastructure; the connections within neighborhoods, connection within the community, is still the most important thing here in Taipei. I think loneliness is a very urban issue. So, to solve loneliness, to actually build up connections within the community, can contribute to resilience.

When people get to know each other, they know when something happened, who is not able to get down the stairs, they know which door to knock on if something happens. That's the thing that I really want to build in our city.

You've argued that China's influence operations against Taiwan are already a form of cognitive warfare. What does that look like in everyday Taiwanese life?

It's not just crude propaganda; it's more about how our daily life might be infiltrated by their information. They can have lively videos talking about cute animals or fortune telling, and so it's very easy for the younger generation to consume that kind of information. But if you click then you're pushed into videos talking about how the U.S. cannot be trusted, Japan is not your friend, and the E.U. is too far away, trying to imply that China is your only friend. It is not just the younger generation, but also elderly people, who are watching all these videos online and could be influenced by all this disinformation.

Taiwan is a proudly open society. How do you guard against manipulation while still allowing for a free media landscape and avoiding censorship?

There are so many ways that you can stop information manipulation. One thing is just to cut off the source, but I don't think it's a good idea. We're an open society, we're a democratic society. You're allowed to consume any kind of information that you like.

Another way is that you try to regulate the social media platform; for example, identification to make sure that there's not so many fake accounts controlled by just one guy, allowing real voices to be disseminated. But I think the best way is still through education, because it's more difficult for them to infiltrate offline.

So, if people are hanging out with each other and discussing conspiracies they saw online, that's the gist of democracy and the best way we can counter information operations.

Some analysts suggest there are thousands of Chinese Communist Party (CCP) operatives in Taiwan. Do you agree with these reports?

For me, it's more about risk management, because let's say businessmen or singers and actors travel to China often. But they're victims, because when they have their business interests over there, they could be threatened by China. We know these guys are traveling to China; they might meet someone from the United Front [CCP overseas influence department] and they need to be protected. It's not like, “hey, they're traveling over there and when they come back we treat them like a spy.” I don't think it's a good idea.

For us, it's all about transparency, and our policy is that when [officials] want to travel to China, you need to report, and the government will tell you, “hey, these are the guys that maybe you don't want to meet,” or if they threaten you, what you could do. In that way, you're protecting your citizens instead of labeling them as “infiltrated by China” so we need to investigate. I don't think it's a good idea to do that.

How vulnerable is Taiwan today to Chinese political influence through business, media, entertainment?

I think media is pretty much the same [as business], because most media are invested by entrepreneurs, and lots have their business in China. So, once you have the business interest there, you might be asked by the Chinese agent, “hey, maybe you should put on some political talk show and try to denounce the current government.” There are journalists being investigated for this kind of situation. So, it's all about how we can protect them at the very beginning instead of punishing them afterwards. Risk management is always a better idea in democratic society.

You've been personally sanctioned by China. How has that changed your understanding of the threat?

When we talk about information operations, it could be online activities. The other thing is offline activities; if someone has been proactively approached by China, which may ask him to do something. But to politicians or to the military, it's called psychological warfare. They want to put pressure on you and make sure that you make wrong decisions. So, they sanction me and try to say, “hey, if you travel abroad, I will arrest you.” However, because I’ve got a public profile it's much easier for me to deal with that pressure. But there are the other guys who do not [have such a profile]: the Uyghurs, or the Hong Kong dissidents. All these guys are facing the same pressure.

So, the first thing is that we need to unify. And second is to show we're not afraid. When they said they want to arrest me if I travel abroad, only two days later I traveled to Germany, the Netherlands, and France, because I want to prove that it's not a real thing. That's the spirit I also want to show to Taiwanese people but also other people all around the world that have been sanctioned or threatened by China.

You mentioned some European countries, but would you still feel secure traveling to places more in Beijing's orbit, such as Thailand or Cambodia?

Thailand, Cambodia, maybe Malaysia—they all have a record that they send human rights defenders or dissidents back to China, so it's not really safe to travel.

Taiwanese cities traditionally have a history of cultural exchanges and informal ties with Chinese cities. Is this something that you would continue if you were elected mayor of Taipei?

For [over ten years,] there’s been the Twin City Forum between Taipei and Shanghai. But first, we're the capital, so I think we should have the forum with Beijing. That's one thing. But what really happens between Taipei and Shanghai is that everyone sits down and reads some memos and takes some good pictures. For me, it doesn't really contribute to anything. And another thing is that China is the country that wants to invade Taiwan, so let's say if you want to exchange some transportation data, that might be a little sensitive, so there should be some risk management. So I won't say all this should be cut off, but it needs to be efficient, it needs more participation, and we need risk management, and then we [also] need to collaborate with other cities.

How important is maintaining Taiwan's leadership of the global tech ecosystem for island security?

That's super important. Nvidia’s [new global headquarters] is coming to northern Taipei, but it's not just about the company and the technology, it's more about the talent, the people. So, you want to make Taipei an easy city for any talents so people want to stay here, and to do that you need companies, but you also need information delivered to all the companies of the world that, “hey, Taipei right now is ready.” It's not about the rent, the energy, the regulation—these are ready. You're also offering opportunities to the younger generation, to engineers, that they can work in AI. Then you got lots of research ideas coming out, and other companies would say, “hey, maybe we should come here because lots of talent live here in the city.” How to make that happen is crucial.

KMT Chairperson Cheng Li-wun recently went to Beijing and met with Xi Jinping. Was that a positive move for Taiwanese people?

Definitely not. It's not a good move for Taiwan, because China is the country that wants to invade Taiwan, and they're also pushing more gray zone tactics against Taiwan, and they're trying to hack more infrastructure here in Taiwan. They never stop.

You have a signed Ukrainian flag behind you. What did your trip to Ukraine teach you about the political reality here in Taiwan and the risks you face?

I visited there when I was a scholar in 2023, so I was not a legislator at that time. But I was invited by their government. I also had lots of exchanges with their NGOs. I really want to see how they build up that kind of resilience. I learned so many things, but first is how they try to counter disinformation. And even in 2023, drones were already super important. I visited some drone factories and saw they needed some components, as lots of components are exported by China, and then when China tried to cut off these components it made Ukraine more vulnerable. So that is why the U.S. and also Japan are talking about “non-red” supply chains. You still need to build up this kind of international collaboration among all these democratic countries, because we need to fight together. 

China also tries to spread a lot of this disinformation against Ukraine, saying that Ukraine is the one that triggered the war, and Ukraine's like so violent they tried to kill lots of Russians. So if we never collaborate with each other, we just let all these conspiracies spread. International collaboration is the only way we can counter [disinformation]—because all these authoritarians already collaborate with each other.

We're now in the third consecutive term of DPP government and relations with China have continued to worsen. How can the DPP make Taiwan safer if it has zero dialogue with Beijing?

Some direct channels would still be very important. Back in the Cold War, even the U.S. and Russia still had connections. Without that connection, something bad might happen. We want to build a connection, but China is refusing. So if they try to cut off [communications], if they still want to invade Taiwan, the only way to protect us is having our air defense system, having our drones ready, because you still need peace through strength. That's the message we try to deliver to our own citizens.

item.title: Trump Gives ‘America’s Mayor’ the Presidential Medal of Freedom
item.description: Rudy Giuliani rose to national prominence after 9/11 and later helped lead Trump’s effort to overturn the 2020 election results.

media:content.media:credit: Adam Gray–AP Photo/Bloomberg via Getty Images
media:content.media:description: Rudy Giuliani, the former mayor of New York, arrives ahead of the 25th anniversary commemoration ceremony at the National 9/11 Memorial and Museum in New York on Sept. 11, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump on Tuesday presented Rudy Giuliani, the former Mayor of New York City who served as Trump’s personal lawyer in 2020, with the Presidential Medal of Freedom. 

Appearing on Steve Bannon’s War Room podcast on Monday, Giuliani said that he was “very, very humbled and very honored” by the recognition. 

Giuliani rose to prominence as a prosecutor in New York and was first elected Mayor of New York City in 1993 as a Republican. For his leadership during 9/11, he was dubbed “America’s Mayor.” In 2007, he launched a bid for the presidency but withdrew after placing third in the Florida primary in January 2008. 

Giuliani went on to become one of Trump’s closest allies, serving first as an adviser and later as his personal lawyer.

Read more: Rudy Giuliani's Past Explains His More Recent Behavior With Trump, Documentary Argues

Following the 2020 presidential election, Giuliani helped lead Trump’s effort to overturn the results in key battleground states, spreading false claims of widespread voter fraud. He was widely identified as an unindicted co-conspirator in the federal election interference case against Trump and faced separate state charges in Georgia and Arizona. Both state cases were dismissed, though Arizona prosecutors can refile charges. In November 2025, Trump pardoned Giuliani for federal offenses related to the 2020 election. The pardon did not extend to state charges.

Giuliani was also disbarred in New York and Washington, D.C. He settled a defamation suit brought by Dominion Voting Systems and reached a separate settlement with two Georgia election workers who had won a $148 million defamation judgment against him.

Trump announced in September on Truth Social last year that he would be awarding Giuliani the Presidential Medal of Freedom, days after Giuliani was hospitalized with a fractured vertebra and other injuries from a car crash in New Hampshire. Trump presented the medal nearly 15 months after announcing it, with two recipients awarded in the meantime. In the post, Trump hailed Giuliani as “the greatest mayor in the history of New York City, and an equally great American Patriot.”

The Presidential Medal of Freedom is the highest civilian honor in the U.S. and recognizes an individual's contributions to the security or national interests of the United States, to world peace, or to cultural or other significant public or private endeavors. The award was established by President John F. Kennedy in 1963, expanding on an existing Medal of Freedom that honored wartime civilian service. Two weeks after Kennedy’s assassination, President Lyndon B. Johnson presented the first Presidential Medals of Freedom on Dec. 6, 1963, and included a posthumous award for Kennedy.

Who has received Trump’s Presidential Medal of Freedom?

Giuliani is the second Presidential Medal of Freedom recipient of 2026 and the third since Trump returned to the White House. 

In October 2025, political activist Charlie Kirk was also awarded the medal posthumously after he was fatally shot in Utah. In September 2026, Trump posthumously awarded the medal to Welles Crowther, an equities trader who became known as the “man in the red bandanna” after rescuing several people in the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. 

During his State of the Union address in February, Trump announced that he would award the medal to Connor Hellebuyck, which would make him the first individual hockey player to receive it. TIME has reached out to the White House about the anticipated timeline for Hellebuyck’s award.

Trump has awarded 27 Presidential Medals of Freedom across two terms so far. The Congressional Research Service counted 26 before Giuliani’s award, compared with 57 under Joe Biden and 118 under Barack Obama. While the award is traditionally nonpartisan and based on individual merit, recipients under the Trump Administration have largely featured conservative politicians and donors, activists, and athletes. A majority of his recipients were recognized for accomplishments in sports. Conservative radio host Rush Limbaugh, Republican Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio, golfer Tiger Woods, and businesswoman Miriam Adelson were among the honorees during his first term, which also featured a posthumous recognition for Elvis Presley.

Two people are known to have declined to receive Trump’s Presidential Medals of Freedom. Country singer Dolly Parton said in 2021 that she had twice declined the offer from Trump, citing her husband’s illness and concerns about traveling during the pandemic. Football coach Bill Belichick also declined the offer following the Jan. 6 attacks on the Capitol.

item.title: Habits Food-Waste Experts Recommend This Thanksgiving
item.description: How to plan your Thanksgiving menu to avoid food waste.

media:content.media:description: Thanksgiving food is often about abundance—but that can often lead to a lot of food waste.

item.content:encoded:
For millions around the country, Thanksgiving preparations are in full swing. But after we fill up on turkey and countless sides, what’s left often goes to waste. 

One study found that, in 2025, Americans discarded enough food to fill 40 football fields from their Thanksgiving meals. We spoke with experts about how you can avoid food waste this Thanksgiving. 

Read more: Will Bad Weather Disrupt Thanksgiving Travel?

Make a realistic plan before you shop

Avoiding food waste starts long before your meal is on the table. Before you go shopping, look through your kitchen to see what you already have. 

As you plan your groceries, think through how much food you’ll need. “Really be realistic about how many people are coming to your gathering and try to get as accurate as you can about how much food you need,” says Robin McClave, program director for the Healthy Schools, Healthy Communities initiative at American University. “Thanksgiving in general, we usually find that people try to prepare in abundance, but then don't necessarily have a plan for the leftovers. A lot of extra food was served intentionally just to have abundance, but also unintentionally because they weren't sure how much food would be consumed.”

Make sure the items you’re making are things your guests will enjoy. “Plan for the likes and dislikes of the folks around the table,” said Norbert Wilson, director of the World Food Policy Center at Duke University. “If your group doesn’t like sweet potato casserole with pecans, or there are allergies to nuts, then do not make it or make a smaller version for the folks who like it.” 

Read more: 13 Habits Food-Waste Experts Practice in Their Own Kitchens

Wilson also recommends using a sign up sheet if you’re hosting a potluck, to ensure you don’t end up just eating mashed potatoes all night. 

And if you’re not cooking for a big group, consider using canned or frozen vegetables that can be easily saved and stored for later, McClave adds. 

Be practical—and creative—with your leftovers

Don’t toss out any trimmings—they can easily be used to make a future meal. “If there's ways to use peels or trimmings like bones from turkey or other proteins, for example, you can also save those to make stock that you can use for soups and other items later,” says Brenna Ellison,  professor of agribusiness management at Purdue University.  

Encourage guests to bring Tupperware to help make leftovers more manageable. “The food is more likely to get utilized across everyone, and then it's not just the host’s responsibility to come up with solutions for all the food,” says Ellison.

If you’re tired of turkey, freeze leftovers to eat later. “If you're not someone that has a ready-to-go plan to use the leftovers immediately, also think about, can we freeze some of them and store them to where we can have a planned use for them in the future?” says Ellison. “So then you're also saving yourself money down the road if you can incorporate those dishes into another meal later.” 

Otherwise, Ellison recommends getting creative with your leftovers—and maybe making new memories along the way. “I have a friend whose family always makes turkey tetrazzini the next day with leftover turkey, for example,” says Ellison, “and that's also part of their tradition that they get really excited about.”

item.title: 'We Don’t Report to the U.S.': Canada Pushes Back Against Public Rebuke From Pentagon
item.description: The Pentagon claimed Canada is prioritizing domestic economic interests over military effectiveness.

media:content.media:description: Canada's Minister of National Defence David McGuinty speaks during a meeting with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at the Pentagon on Sept. 22, 2025.

item.content:encoded:
Canada’s Minister of National Defense David McGuinty on Tuesday emphasized his country’s sovereignty as he pushed back against the Pentagon’s accusation that Ottawa is falling short as a credible partner in defending North America. 

"Canada's a sovereign nation. I'll be very direct. We don't report to the United States,” he told reporters, when asked about the Pentagon’s public rebuke. “I cannot explain the Pentagon's behavior, nor of the Secretary [of Defense.]”

The Pentagon under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth released a two-page fact sheet on Monday, outlining what it described as Canada's “defense shortfalls” and criticizing the country's leadership under Prime Minister Mark Carney.

The document focused on what it characterized as Canada's underinvestment in the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) and its defense spending plan for NATO. Canada joined allies at the 2025 NATO summit at the Hague in pledging to reach 5% of GDP by 2035 in defense spending. The country’s latest budget projects combined defense and security spending of 4.1% of GDP by 2027-28, but Canada’s Parliamentary Budget Officer’s assessment last week stated that the path to reach 5% by 2035 remains “unclear.” The Pentagon, meanwhile, has accused Canada of deferring its largest increases needed to actualize the NATO spending target until after the 2029 federal election.

McGuinty staunchly defended his government’s defense spending plans, arguing that Canada remains on track to reach the 5% target. He argued that NATO allies had agreed to review the spending pledge in 2029.

When asked about the Pentagon’s comments that Canada is not a “credible partner,” McGuinty stressed the continued cooperation between the two neighboring countries. 

"I can’t divine what the thinking is,” he added. “The amount of cooperation that we’re pursuing together under NORAD has not changed. What we’re doing together at NATO has not changed. Our military to military cooperation has not changed."

The Pentagon said Hegseth is “laser focused” on enabling Canada’s military modernization “after decades of American taxpayers footing the bill for its homeland defense.” The rhetoric follows that displayed by President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly accused Canada of “ripping off” the United States

Going a step further, the Pentagon also accused Canadian leaders of prioritizing domestic economic interests over military effectiveness, referencing Ottawa's ongoing review of its planned purchase of American-made F-35 fighter jets, arguing that the uncertainty surrounding the deal could undermine the North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD) cooperation. Carney ordered the review in March 2025, amid an escalating tariffs row and Trump’s repeated threats to annex Canada and make it the “51st state.” The Pentagon said this review, along with Canada’s other alleged shortcomings, has prompted concerns as to whether the country can fulfill its commitments to NORAD, which is jointly operated by the two countries. 

The Pentagon also questioned the readiness of Canada's military, claiming that only 41.9% of its air force fleet and 53.9% of its naval fleet were serviceable in 2025-26, while army readiness stood at 48%. The document framed these items as a burden on U.S. taxpayers.

Canada had previously emphasized its commitment to cooperating with the U.S. on matters of defense. 

“As founding members of NATO, Canada and the United States have stood together in support of collective defense since 1949, and for nearly 70 years we have defended North America together through NORAD, the world’s only binational command,” a spokesperson for the office of McGuinty told TIME on Tuesday, prior to the minister’s comments to reporters. “Canada will continue to do its part to defend North America, as we keep having constructive discussions with our American partners on how best to strengthen our shared defense and security.”

Canada also announced over the weekend that it will join European NATO allies in exploring a pilot project in Keflavík, Iceland, as part of a proposed logistics network to support maritime patrols and anti-submarine operations in the North Atlantic and Arctic.

The move comes as Canada seeks to reduce its reliance on the U.S. by expanding its economic relationships and alliances with other countries. Carney has notably pursued a closer partnership with the European Union, and has laid out his vision for Canada becoming an “associate” member of the bloc. Both sides have expressed openness to a deeper cooperation in critical sectors including defense, technology, and AI.

While some of Canada’s international relationships are flourishing, the public tensions with the U.S. over defense priorities could have a negative impact on future alliances, experts argue.

“Our greatest advantages are the NATO and NORAD alliances, and we are looking to provide support to other partners,” says Andrea Charron, the director of the Centre for Defense and Security Studies at the University of Manitoba in Canada. “This kind of public shaming of a very close and important ally sends a chilling effect throughout all the allyships and partnerships that again serves no one but the adversaries.”

Typically, adversaries of the U.S. and Canada are “always looking for evidence of fractures in the allied relationship,” she adds, noting that now those people can “quote the Secretary of Defense.”

The release of the fact sheet follows a report by the Washington Post last week that said Hegseth had circulated a classified memorandum imposing new restrictions on military cooperation with Canada.

McGuinty responded to the report by saying he had not seen the memorandum and had no evidence of any changes to military cooperation between the two countries.

Joseph Jockel, a professor of Canadian studies at St. Lawrence University, says the noise around the memo regarding restrictions is “the second symbolic warning that [the U.S.] has sent Ottawa.” The first came in May, he says, when the Defense Department paused U.S. participation with Canada on the Permanent Joint Board on Defence (PJBD), a long-standing low profile mechanism for discussions on U.S.-Canada defense coordination.

“It sent a strong symbolic gesture, and now they're doing the same thing, they're looking for symbolic steps,” he argues.  

Republican Senator Mike Rounds of South Dakota, a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, sought to downplay the significance of the reported restrictions, suggesting they were largely symbolic and would not affect day-to-day military operations, intelligence sharing, or defense planning.

“They’re basically limiting some social engagements, and they’re asking people to get permission before they come in and do think tanks and so forth,” he said at the Halifax International Security Forum on Nov. 21. “We don’t expect any real changes over the way it has been going for the last year or a year and a half.”

Chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell told TIME that the Department of Defense “is taking steps to ensure its engagements with Canada advance tangible U.S. defense objectives and ultimately support a reinvigorated defense relationship."

“This guidance does not impact defense intelligence cooperation, our binational NORAD command, or our cooperation through NATO,” he added.

Despite those reassurances, the developments have raised concerns about the future of the countries' longstanding defense relationship.

Canadian Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre said Sunday that any “restrictions on Canada-U.S. military cooperation by the Administration” would amount to a "terrible" mistake.

U.S.-Canada rift grows as trade war stretches on

The Pentagon's public criticism of Canada's military capabilities and leadership comes as relations between the two countries remain strained by an ongoing trade war, with negotiations stalled and no clear path toward a deal.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told Fox News over the weekend that the two sides were having “constructive conversations” and had “made a lot of progress,” but raised concerns over Canada's decision to lower tariffs on a quota of Chinese electric vehicles and provide relief for certain Chinese steel and aluminum imports.

Carney's pivot toward China and the trade alliances drawn up between the two countries have also drawn criticism from Trump.

Experts tell TIME that the growing economic relationship could potentially give Ottawa greater leverage in future trade negotiations with Washington.

item.title: 11 Things People in Healthy Relationships Say to Each Other
item.description: 'Let me try that again.'

media:content.media:credit: Photo-Illustration by TIME (Source Image: DAJ/Getty Images)

item.content:encoded:
No one teaches you how to talk to your partner. You pick it up as you go—sometimes by watching your family members, sometimes by saying the wrong thing and wishing you could rewind. But listen to people in healthy relationships, and certain kinds of words come up again and again: the ones that show appreciation, make room for a bad day, or let someone know they don’t have to hide the messy parts of being human.

“Sometimes people just want to feel seen,” says Stephanie Michaelian, a Los Angeles-based therapist. That’s part of what makes these words matter: They show a partner you’re paying attention, whether they’re having a hard day or celebrating something they worked hard to achieve.

We asked therapists to share what, exactly, people in healthy relationships say to each other—and the small but meaningful signals behind them.

“I never thought about it that way.”

A partner’s perspective can change yours. That’s the point of this line, says Maggie Vaughan, a licensed marriage and family therapist. It shows you’re not just waiting for your turn to talk; you’re taking their point seriously enough to consider it. Vaughan says that can help a partner feel “seen in the ways that they would like to see themselves, almost as though it’s a non-physical embrace.”

“Do you want me to listen, problem-solve, or just be here with you in this?”

When someone starts talking about their hard day, it’s easy to assume they want advice. But jumping straight to solutions can make your partner feel as if their emotions are a problem to be fixed. Emotional attunement, on the other hand, means being present with what your partner is feeling instead of trying to make the feeling disappear.

You don’t have to agree with their take on what happened, Michaelian says; you can simply acknowledge its impact: “I see that this impacted you, and that sounds hard.” She calls that “so, so loving”—“being in a feeling with them rather than just trying to make it go away or trying to fix it.” Asking first gives your partner room to say what would actually help, and sometimes they may not know until they’ve had a chance to talk.

“Help me understand what that was like for you.”

When your partner tells you that something you said or did hurt them, it’s easy to jump in with context: That’s not what I meant. But Erika Bach, founder and clinical director of the New York psychotherapy practice You, Me, says their hurt gives you “the opportunity to understand what it was like for them and to repair.” The question tells your partner you’re ready to hear them out: “I want to understand this,” she says. “You matter to me.” Let your partner tell you how it landed before the two of you get into what you intended.

“I can see you’re not feeling your best today. Let me take care of dinner tonight. I want to take something off your plate.”

Clearly, this is a kind offer—but the steaming container of takeout is only part of it. The subtext is that your partner noticed you were running on empty and wanted to make the evening easier. “That by itself, even without the second part, can be really loving and helpful,” Michaelian says. “I notice you. I’m paying attention to you.” If you’re overwhelmed, you might not have the energy to ask for help; knowing your partner has noticed can matter even more than having your favorite dinner on the table.

“I know this is hard, and I am so proud of you.”

Your partner doesn’t have to be in crisis to need your support. Vaughan says it can mean a lot to know you see the effort behind something they’re excited about, too. “Sometimes it’s easier to support someone when they’re down than when they’re up,” she says. “But our partners need us when we’re up too.”

“Thank you for telling me. I know that wasn’t easy.”

When your partner tells you that something you did hurt them, they’re trusting you with a vulnerable part of themselves. Bach describes opening up as “a risk and a gift.” Thanking them for telling you acknowledges that trust. “I appreciate the fact that you’re willing to let me in on your inner world,” she says. “It’s kind of inviting them to do it again and again.” The hurt still needs to be addressed, but your partner knows you’re not brushing them off.

“You don’t have to be in a good mood for me to want to be around you.”

Nobody wants to feel like they have to put on a happy face to be loved. “Sometimes people feel really pressured to regulate their emotions really quick,” Michaelian says, or to hide their feelings because they don’t want to feel like a burden. But, she says, “you don’t have to be your best self all the time in order to be loved and accepted.” 

That reassurance is about feelings, however, and not a free pass for how someone treats you. There’s still a line: If a partner is “being mean or abusive,” Michaelian says, “that’s not OK.”

“I got defensive. Let me try that again.”

People get defensive. The useful part is being able to catch it—and start over. Bach says acknowledging your reaction shows self-awareness and accountability. “It’s a real positive marker for change and growth,” she says. You don’t have to come up with a perfect response on the first try; you do have to be willing to notice when you’ve stopped listening.

“I’ve been missing spending quality time with you. Could we plan an evening just for us this week?”

“You never make time for us” is a pretty efficient way to start an argument about schedules. Michaelian says the feeling underneath may actually be: “I miss you, and I want to feel close to you. I want to know that spending time together is important to you.” That gives the two of you something to work with: maybe cooking dinner with both phones put away, instead of debating who’s had the busier week.

“I need a few minutes, and I’m coming back.”

Sometimes stepping away is the only way to keep an argument from getting worse. But “I can’t do this” can come across as “I’m breaking up with you,” Bach says. Instead, offer a specific return plan: “Give me 20 minutes. Let’s keep talking about this.” It gives both people room to cool off and tells your partner the conversation still matters. Then come back when you said you would, she adds.

“We disagree on this, and I still love you.”

You and your partner will never see everything the same way. Couples can revisit the same issue “over and over and over again,” Vaughan says. “And that’s OK.” You can disagree about something without making it a verdict on the whole relationship. “We can be on the same team, we can respect each other, we can love each other,” Vaughan says. “A disagreement over one perspective does not change the fact that I adore 98% of you.”

item.title: Representative Jimmy Gomez Resigns After House Ethics Panel Finds Evidence of Sexual Misconduct
item.description: Gomez is the second Democrat from California to resign from Congress this year following sexual misconduct allegations.

media:content.media:description: Representative Jimmy Gomez, a Democrat from California, during a House Intelligence Committee hearing on worldwide threats in Washington, D.C, on March 19, 2026.

item.content:encoded:
Representative Jimmy Gomez, a California Democrat, announced his resignation Monday after a House ethics panel found “substantial evidence” that he engaged in sexual misconduct.

Gomez, in a statement, said he “recognize[s] the seriousness of the Ethics Committee’s report,” but has “strong disagreements” with its conclusions. “Among other significant deficiencies and omissions, the report does not include key portions of my testimony that are essential to a full and fair understanding of what occurred,” Gomez said.

He also criticized the process of the investigation, which began after a report of him kissing an aide emerged in April. “With this in mind, I see no other alternative than to resign, effective December 1, to allow for my staff to close out important constituent casework and needs,” he added.

Gomez has represented California’s 34th district since 2017, after winning a special election to succeed Xavier Becerra, who at the time was appointed the state's Attorney General after Kamala Harris was elected to the Senate. Gomez was already set to leave office in early 2027, after losing his re-election bid to newcomer Angela Gonzales-Torres.

But his resignation just weeks before the congressional turnover would make Gomez the second California Democratic lawmaker to resign from his congressional seat this year amid sexual misconduct allegations. In April, former Representative Eric Swalwell, who was then eyeing the governor’s seat and had Gomez as his campaign co-chair, resigned days after allegations of his sexual misconduct surfaced.

Congress has faced renewed scrutiny over its apparent failures to stop abuses of power and to police inappropriate behavior following a spate of sexual misconduct allegations leveled against its members.

The House ethics panel earlier this year also found that Republican Representative Chuck Edwards of North Carolina acted inappropriately toward staffers. Edwards’ colleagues voted to censure him, following the panel’s recommendations. Ahead of the vote, Edwards wrote a six-page letter to other House members defending himself. Representative Cory Mills, a Florida Republican, also faces an ongoing ethics probe over allegations of sexual and financial misconduct. Mills, who has denied the allegations, lost a primary election earlier this year.

Hakeem Jeffries, the House Democratic leader set to be Speaker after Congress flipped blue, said in a joint statement with his fellow party leaders that the report on Gomez was “serious and deeply troubling” and that his resignation was “appropriate.” The leaders added that “decisive action to set a new standard for reform is an urgent priority for House Democrats,” as they take over Congress next year.

What were the allegations against Gomez?

While Swalwell’s controversy made headlines in April, the New York Post reported that Gomez was seen “surreptitiously kissing a much younger congressional aide in the summer of 2023.” According to the report, the incident happened outside a backyard party hosted by Swalwell “to celebrate the start of the August congressional recess.”

Gomez had resigned as co-chair of Swalwell’s California gubernatorial campaign after the allegations against his colleague emerged, which he called “shocking.”

According to the Ethics Committee’s report, on May 6, Gomez, who is married, disclosed through counsel that he had “a past consensual, sexual relationship with a senior employee in the personal office of a more senior Member of Congress,” and “one sole occasion” of “consensual kissing with a senior employee of another, more senior Member’s office.”

The ethics panel reached out to both female employees. The first denied nonconsensual sexual interactions with Gomez. But the second female employee, who was in her mid-20s and worked in the House for years before leaving in 2025, told the committee that she had more than one physical encounter with Gomez, both of which she did not consider consensual.

The woman first met Gomez in 2018, but had little interaction with him, according to the committee report. She had her first “meaningful interaction” with Gomez at a Feb. 29, 2024 birthday party hosted by another congressional member in a bar near Capitol Hill. She and Gomez left the party with the unspecified lawmaker and another unidentified woman for a Chinatown bar.

According to the report, the woman told the panel that while they were at the Chinatown bar, Gomez started to touch her legs, adding: “he put his hand down my skirt and then put his fingers inside of me.” She said the incident was nonconsensual.

Later outside the bar, the woman said Gomez pushed her against a wall and kissed her, and she said she “kissed him back because I just wanted to go home and I just, like, wanted it to end.” Gomez, according to the report, recalled that he made sexual contact with the woman only once they were outside the bar. 

The second encounter happened in July 2024, according to the woman. She told the panel that during an evening vote series in the House, she texted Gomez and met up with him at his office upon his invitation. They talked, but she eventually felt uncomfortable and made a motion to leave, but as she was about to leave, Gomez tried to kiss her in a “pretty forceful” manner.

“I opened the door, and he grabbed my arm and he, like, grabbed my body and, like, pushed it into his and started caressing my back and, like, put his hand on my face and, like, tried to kiss me,” she said. 

Gomez testified that he had walked her to the door and bid her goodbye, to which the woman reacted “fine.” He also told the panel that he did not try to kiss her on the lips; that besides a hug, he did not put his hands on her; and that no signs showed her discomfort with the interaction.

The panel found that the interactions with the former female employee “constitute sexual misconduct in violation of House Rules and merit consideration by the full House.” The committee report said that Gomez’s conduct “at various junctures suggests he knew that what he was doing was wrong,” and that his actions towards her “could implicate D.C. laws related to criminal sexual assault, including misdemeanor sexual abuse.” But the committee did not recommend any punishment for Gomez, citing his re-election loss.

What are the reactions?

Lawyers for the woman at the heart of the allegations against Gomez lauded the Ethics Committee for its handling of the investigation.

“However, Representative Gomez’s conduct did not occur in a vacuum, and immediate steps must be taken by Congress to rein in what the report describes as a ‘toxic and predatory culture,’” her attorneys Lisa J. Banks and Sarah E. Nesbitt said in a statement. “Democracy cannot function properly when women must endure harassment and abuse as a condition of public service.”

Gonzales-Torres, who defeated Gomez in the midterms, criticized him for not resigning sooner and told the Los Angeles Times on Monday that the accusations against him “reflect a broader environment of sexual misconduct and toxic working conditions on Capitol Hill.” 

Last week, the House Ethics Committee adopted rule changes to fast-track and improve transparency related to sexual misconduct probes, amid pressure brought on by the increase in allegations.

Representative Teresa Leger Fernández of New Mexico, who chairs the Democratic Women’s Caucus, called Gomez’s actions “reprehensible and a gross abuse of power” and thanked the Ethics Committee for its investigation, which forced the embattled California lawmaker to resign instead of facing a motion to expel him from the chamber. 

GOP Representative Kat Cammack of Florida, who, alongside Leger Fernández, co-chairs the bipartisan task force aimed at changing the way Congress handles sexual harassment claims, said that while resigning is the “right call,” it cannot “begin and end” there.

“This is bigger than one member,” Cammack said. “Misconduct and toxic working conditions still fester in too many offices on Capitol Hill, and we can’t keep responding after the fact.”

item.title: Jensen Huang and the Cult of the Male Tech Founder
item.description: What experts say Jensen Huang’s comeback reveals about gender and power in Silicon Valley.
item.content:encoded:
Even by Silicon Valley's standards, Jensen Huang’s scandals were outlandish. Huang resigned two weeks ago following reports that he had an affair with tech executive Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy whose company was suspected of steering restricted advanced AI chips to the country.  He has also reportedly engaged in at least two other affairs with subordinates at Nvidia and was known for belittling those who worked under him. 

While Huang’s controversies have been unusually shocking for an industry whose real-life corporate dramas often create the plotlines of Hollywood blockbusters, his return to helm the CEO position at Nvidia is not. 

For decades, tech founders have left their companies amid managerial or ethical controversies, only to be brought back by supporters who argue they alone contain the ability and vision to lead the companies they created. Experts who study the industry refer to this as the “cult of the founder”—the idea that entrepreneurs should be given wide latitude to grow their transformative companies, even if that means their employees and the marketplace are forced to accept some of their obvious leadership flaws.

“Nvidia is too big to fail and Nvidia will fail without Jensen at the helm—that's the message this seems to be sending,” says Margaret O’Mara, a professor of history at the University of Washington, who has studied the tech sector.  

Yet, the cultural and political support behind Huang and other male founders takes place in an industry in which women leaders have struggled to obtain promotions and investment for their companies, and are often held to higher standards of behavior when they occupy those roles. Other times, they are brought in to rescue companies already plagued with problems  that other executives failed to solve such as when Yahoo tapped former Google executive Marissa Mayer as CEO in 2012.   

The tech sector tends to uphold the views of male founders to chart the path for the industry, while relying on female executives to fix issues inside companies, says Bhaskar Chakravorti, dean of global business at The Fletcher School at Tufts University.  

Read More: 6 Questions About Jensen Huang's Stunning Return as Nvidia CEO

Huang’s origin story had the markings of a classic Silicon Valley success tale. A Taiwanese immigrant, Huang founded Nvidia after getting into a conversation with two other engineers at a Denny’s diner about building a computer chip that would improve video game graphics. Huang, who often touted his prior work as a busboy at Denny’s, later founded and grew the company to become a lynchpin of America’s AI boom by selling graphics processing units that make training AI models faster. 

The effects of Huang’s departure were swift. Earlier this month, Nvidia’s board tapped chief financial officer Colette Kress to be interim CEO, and said it would initiate an independent investigation into reports that Huang was the subject of a foreign intelligence effort.  Not only did Nvidia’s stock plunge following the announcement of Huang’s departure, it also dragged down the S&P 500, which has benefited from investors’ excitement about artificial intelligence.

While many regulators and advocates supported Huang’s departure, a cohort of influential tech industry leaders publicly urged the board to reinstate him including Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, hedge fund manager Bill Ackman, Epic Games founder and CEO Tim Sweeney, and many Nvidia employees.  The “Stand with Jensen” campaign argued that “accountability requires evidence, a fair hearing, and a reasoned decision. Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice.” 

Huang also had the backing of President Donald Trump’s administration, urging the board to reinstate the executive after assuring them that he was not facing criminal charges, nor did he pose a national security risk, according to the New York Times.  Alice Huang’s former company, Megaspeed, is being investigated by federal agencies, alongside a probe  initiated by Nvidia’s board of directors. As the campaign to bring Huang back expanded, the founder himself indicated earlier this month that he would welcome the opportunity to return to the role.

“It's hard for me to imagine a woman CEO even getting to that position of prominence, and it's even harder for me to imagine a woman CEO doing what Huang did, and then also having this sort of comeback,” says Mar Hicks, an associate professor at the University of Virginia. 

“There isn't much precedent for that, and it's definitely the case that generally women, and in particular, women of color are held to much, much higher standards, and oftentimes don't even have to do anything wrong to lose their jobs or lose their positions of prominence or lose respect.” 

The tech industry commonly embraces the idea that founders are critical to the success of their companies. Tech leaders such as Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg have relied on a dual-class share structure that gives them majority voting power.  Some VCs have sought to cast themselves as being founder-friendly by refraining from criticizing or firing them, in part to gain a competitive edge in the market.  Prominent investors have argued that founders often have judgment that surpasses that of their reports, and therefore should take a hands-on role in running their companies even as they grow bigger. 

Nvidia’s board had their pick of examples in which bringing back a founder to lead a tech company was seen to boost its performance. Michael Dell stepped down as CEO in 2004 only to return to the role three years later, and has since repositioned Dell to take advantage of the artificial intelligence boom.  Steve Jobs famously was ousted from his role at Apple in 1985 during a power struggle with the board and then-CEO John Sculley, only to return as CEO more than a decade later when the company was struggling. Jobs was seen to have rescued the company, partly with a wave of new product launches that transformed personal computing, including the iPod, iPhone, and App Store. More recently, OpenAI’s board of directors fired founder and CEO Sam Altman in 2023, only for the company to bring him back less than a week later after intense pressure from employees and outside investors. 

After news surfaced that Huang was returning as CEO, Nvidia's stock surged on Monday by more than 30%. Haung’s return supports the idea “that these people are too important and these companies are too economically consequential, so we're just going to forgive. We are going to forgive these things because this is the price of doing business,”  O’Mara says.

item.title: Mamdani Unveils Plan to Close Infamous Rikers Island, Replace It With ‘Borough-Based Jails’ by 2032. How Would It Work?
item.description: In the place of the notorious jail complex, the city is set to open “borough-based” jails in Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, and the Bronx.
item.content:encoded:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has announced plans to  shut down the city’s Rikers Island jail complex in 2032 after a century in operation, setting an end date for a site that has long been infamous for persistent violence and abuse.

In its place, the city is set to open “borough-based” jails in four of its five boroughs: Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, and the Bronx. The fifth, Staten Island, would be the only borough not to host a jail.

“Our administration is closing Rikers Island once and for all, and building a city where we ask ourselves what a person needs, not just what they're accused of, and in its place, we will open four borough-based jails starting in 2029,” Mamdani said in a video announcement last week. 

Rikers Island, which serves as the primary facility where people are held while awaiting trial or serving short sentences in the city, has been plagued for decades by reports of violence by both inmates and correctional officers, deaths in custody, a lack of oversight, and decrepit conditions.

New York City lawmakers previously laid out a decade-long plan to shutter the Rikers complex and replace it with borough-based jails in 2017. The city council passed legislation two years later that legally required that change to be enacted by September 2027—a deadline that Mamdani’s plan is now set to move back by five years.

Mamdani said that the new timeline was “made necessary by the prior administration’s delays” at a press conference last week. Former Mayor Eric Adams, who preceded Mamdani in the office, supported closing down Rikers, but opposed the idea of borough-based jails to house its inmates. 

Here’s what to know about the borough-based jail model, the impact it could have on New York City’s prison population, and what challenges Mamdani could face in seeking to make the shift.

What is Mamdani’s plan?

Mamdani’s plan seeks to replace the Rikers complex with borough-based jails that are “safer and more humane, in locations closer to courts and public transportation to improve access to court dates, attorneys, service providers and visits,” according to the city’s website. 

The Brooklyn jail is set to open in 2029, followed by the jails in the Bronx and Queens—which will be an all-women facility—in 2031 and the final jail in Manhattan in 2032. 

The new jails will be designed to be “safer and easier to supervise” compared to Rikers, with fewer beds per housing unit, according to the Mayor’s office. Mamdani said during his video announcement of the plan that this “will help correctional staff better protect those in custody.”

The four new jails will cost an estimated $15 billion to build, according to the plan. A report from the Independent Rikers Commission from 2025 estimated that once up and running, a borough-based system would save the city $2.4 billion in operating and overtime costs. 

To accomplish the move to such a system, Mamdani’s plan aims to reduce the city’s jail population from its current level of 6,600 inmates to no more than 5,500 by the time the first borough-based jail is anticipated to open in 2029, and no more than 4,100 by the end of 2032. 

Mamdani intends to reduce the city’s jail population by working with courts and prosecutors to shorten pre-trial wait times, making it easier to pay bail, implementing incarceration alternative programs, moving inmates with serious mental health or complex medical needs to hospitals, and reducing recidivism rates. 

“We are putting forward this plan in 2026 and doing so on the basis of what we’ve been able to accomplish in the first 11 months of our administration,” Mamdani told The New York Times in an interview. “Accomplishments that have given us the faith of what we’ll be able to do over the next five to six years.”

What are the advantages of the planned change?

Proponents of the borough-based model argue that it would solve one of the Rikers complex’s fundamental flaws: its location. 

The island sits in the city’s East River just north of LaGuardia Airport, with only one bridge connecting it to the mainland, which former Rikers officials and inmates say restricts those inside from making it to court appearances and seeing their families, while limiting the amount of health resources that make it to the island and the oversight the complex receives. 

“There's one very glaring issue, which is that Rikers is a penal colony,” Homer Venters, who served as the chief medical officer of New York City jails from 2015-2017, tells TIME. “That physical separation combined with the decrepit condition of the facilities on the island creates barriers to care, to oversight, and certainly to accountability.” 

Venters says that due to Rikers’ location, it is difficult to transport inmates off the island to receive specialty medical treatment or emergency care. It’s also a challenge, he adds, to get emergency medical services on to the island on short notice, which poses a health risk to all of the inmates. 

Oftentimes, inmates would miss appointments or not receive the care they needed immediately because there were not enough officers to transport them, Venters remembers of his time overseeing the facility. “That wasn't one time. It wasn't a handful of times. It was a consistent problem,” he says. The “decrepit nature of the jails,” on Rikers which are “falling down,” he adds, makes it challenging for inmates to receive adequate medical care on the island. 

Another consistent problem with the jail complex “has been lack of access for visiting family members and loved ones,” adds Venters, who describes family visitation as an “essential service,” along with better access to court hearings and healthcare. “That outweighs the problems and concerns that are raised with using property in the city for a jail.”

Darren Mack, a former Rikers inmate and co-director of the Freedom Agenda, which seeks to decarcerate and transform the prison system, similarly cites the remoteness of Rikers as the source of many of its core issues, including violence against inmates. 

“It takes hours to get there, it takes hours to go see a person for one hour visit,” Mack says. “The isolation, the remoteness of it is what breeds the culture of a violence because it's like out of sight, out of mind.”

The borough-based model, in contrast with the Rikers complex, is designed to keep inmates closer to home, so that they can more easily see their families and also travel shorter distances to court appearances and hospitals.

“To the extent that a city is going to incarcerate people, it is both better for the city and also better for those individuals and their families to have close proximity to the courts,” Venters says. 

What potential challenges could the plan face?

Critics of Mamdani’s plan argue that the borough-based jails will not be able to accommodate the city’s prison population, despite the parts of the plan directly concerned with reducing that population in the coming years.

Michel Rempel, an expert of jail reform at John Jay College in New York, tells TIME that Mamdani’s goals for the borough-based jails are possible, but that they will require a high degree of commitment and execution to meet.  

“There are safe and impactful strategies available to the city and to state courts to reduce the jail population to around 4,000 or even lower, so it's possible,” Rempel says. He adds, however, that Mamdani’s proposed strategies need to be “exceptionally well implemented,” if he is to meet his goals. 

New York City courts, Rempel says, are responsible for who ends up at Rikers, where roughly 85% of the inmate population consists of people awaiting trial. But the city can change where those inmates are sent, he says. 

“The city has the power of the purse, and that means the city can invest in programs that can serve as alternatives to pretrial detention,” he says, “where the existence of those programs can then give courts options they didn't have before.”

Charles Lehman, a senior fellow at the right-leaning public policy think-tank the Manhattan Institute, argues that even if Mamdani’s administration succeeds in reducing the inmate population as planned, inevitable fluctuations in the city’s incarceration rate will eventually challenge the capacity of the borough-based jails.

“He still has not come to his senses on the basic mathematical problem of where are you going to put these people,” Lehman tells TIME of the mayor. “New York City is at a historically low level of crime. That will not be true forever. I guarantee it. Crime goes up and down, and so even if the city miraculously produces a 4,100 person average daily population today, when crime goes up, where are you going to put those people?”

Lehman also contends that moving Rikers inmates into the boroughs could present a safety concern for New Yorkers. He doesn’t so much express worry about inmates breaking out, but rather about alternative situations in which he posits it may be difficult to manage an inmate population that is in closer quarters with New York City residents. 

“What if there's a fire in Midtown Manhattan and in the Manhattan borough-based jail, and you have to evacuate a bunch of dangerous criminals into Midtown Manhattan? How do you solve that issue?” he asks.
